# Work with media
Source: https://hyperframes.heygen.com/guides/media

Use footage, images, audio, captions, backgrounds, and color in a HyperFrames project.

Media can come from your project, a captured website, an upload, or a generated
asset. Put anything required for the final result inside the project so preview
and rendering use the same file.

<video aria-label="The five basic moves: import, place, crop, trim, and swap the source" />

Each step adds one attribute on the left and shows the result on the right. The
last one swaps the file entirely — everything else about the scene stays put.

## Start with the role, not the effect

| Media | Give it one main job |
| - | - |
| Product capture | Prove how the product behaves |
| Footage | Carry a person, place, action, or emotion |
| Image | Hold one idea long enough to understand it |
| Voice | Carry the explanation or story |
| Music | Shape pace and tone |
| Sound effect | Reinforce a meaningful action |

More layers do not automatically make a stronger video. If two assets do the
same job, keep the clearer one.

## Bring it into the project

In the browser editor, open **Assets**, choose **Import media**, or drop files into the
panel. Preview the file before placing it on the timeline. You can also ask the
agent to capture a website, prepare supplied footage, generate a derivative, or
copy an approved file into the project.

Use names such as `pricing-page-scroll.mp4` or `customer-logo.svg`. Clear names
make later revisions much easier for both people and agents.

## Prepare only what the result needs

* Trim or crop a source when the unused material slows down review.
* Remove a background when the subject must sit over a designed scene.
* Grade footage when sources visibly disagree or the story needs a deliberate look.
* Generate captions from the real speech, then correct words and timing before styling them.
* Keep narration clear above music and use effects only for specific events.

The original and prepared file should remain easy to distinguish.

## Remember confirmed preferences

The media-use skill records confirmed choices in `.media/preferences.json`.
Concurrent records preserve each choice, including confirmations that promote a
preference to your personal defaults after use in two projects.

Add `.media/*.lock` to the project's `.gitignore`, while keeping
`preferences.json` committed. If recording reports "Settings are locked…",
confirm that no HyperFrames process is recording preferences before deleting
the named lock file and retrying. A locked personal tier leaves the project
record intact and postpones personal promotion until a later record.

## Check the final timeline

Watch once from beginning to end and check:

* the first and last frame of every video clip;
* crop and resolution at the intended output size;
* caption timing against the spoken words;
* voice clarity on ordinary headphones and laptop speakers;
* missing files, temporary URLs, and late-loading media.

## Reuse an approved recipe

Ask the agent to save an approved video's design and storyboard as a named
recipe for later projects. Saving the same name again creates a new version
and archives the previous project version.

If the new version has no `BRIEF.md`, importing that recipe into another
project does not restore the older brief. The earlier brief remains available
in the archived version.

## Choose a media task

> [card] [Images and video](/guides/video-components)
>
> Import, place, replace, trim, and review visual media.

> [card] [Avatar presenter](/guides/avatar-presenter)
>
> Generate or reuse a presenter clip and compose around it.

> [card] [Voice, music, and sound](/guides/voice-and-audio)
>
> Build an understandable audio mix.

> [card] [Remove a background](/guides/remove-background)
>
> Isolate a person from a real image or clip.

> [card] [Color grading](/guides/media-effects#fix-and-grade-the-color)
>
> Correct footage or establish a deliberate look.

> [card] [Media effects](/guides/media-effects)
>
> Apply a non-destructive visual treatment.

## Related topics

* [Use assets and Catalog items in the browser editor](/studio/assets-and-blocks)
* [Finish, render, and share](/guides/export-and-share)


# Add effects to images and video
Source: https://hyperframes.heygen.com/guides/media-effects

Give a photo or video a look (ASCII, halftone, tape damage, CRT, paint) or fix and grade its color, by asking or by hand. The original file never changes.

An effect changes how a picture looks, not what it is. The file stays untouched, so you can soften the effect,
animate it or take it off later.

<video aria-label="Every media effect family, applied to real sources" />

*Eighteen effects, sixteen color looks and four LUT paths, each on one media layer and all still editable.*

## Ask for a look

Say what it should feel like; you don't need the effect names:

```text theme={null}
Make the product clip feel like a clean two-ink editorial print. Keep the label readable.
The interview looks too dark and slightly cold. Keep skin natural, no filtered look.
Pixelate the email address in the screen recording from 0:04 to 0:07.
```

Works the same in the Studio app and with your own agent. To copy a look from a video you like, add it as a
reference and say "grade it like this".

## The effects

* **Essentials:** Blur, Pixelate, Bloom. Hide something, pull focus, make highlights glow.
* **Retro and glitch:** Tape Damage, Film Artifacts, Scanlines, CRT Curvature, Channel Separation, Digital Glitch,
  Chroma Softening. Old tape, old film, old monitors, broken signals, with real tracking wobble and color bleed.
* **Print:** Halftone, Two-Ink Print, Ordered Dither, Mono Screen.
* **Art:** ASCII (eight styles), Engraving, Crosshatch, Kuwahara Paint.

![One presenter frame shown as the original, pixelated, two-ink print, and ASCII treatments](https://static.heygen.ai/hyperframes-oss/docs/images/showcase/media-effects-grid-v1.png)

One source, four finishes: original, pixelated, two-ink print, and ASCII.

Commit to a strong look or leave it off: a half-strength ASCII reads as a mistake. For grain and vignette, use the
color controls below; for HUDs, light leaks and flashes, use a [Catalog overlay](/catalog).

## Fix and grade the color

Correct first (exposure, white balance, contrast, saturation), then style. No look rescues blown highlights or the
wrong shot.

![The same presenter frame before and after a restrained natural portrait grade](https://static.heygen.ai/hyperframes-oss/docs/images/showcase/color-grading-before-after-v1.png)

The same source before and after a restrained natural-portrait grade.

<video aria-label="Correction, presets, curves, selective colour, scopes and a LUT on real footage" />

## Adjust it by hand

In the [browser editor](/studio/index), select an image or video and open **Effects** or **Grade** in the Inspector.
**Grade** starts with thirteen presets, each previewed on your own frame, and a **Strength** slider. Hold the compare
button to flash back to the original, and scrub a few places in moving footage: a grade that flatters one frame can
ruin the next.

| Control | Use it for |
| - | - |
| Preset and strength | Pick a whole look, then dial it back |
| Exposure, contrast, highlights, shadows, whites, blacks | Brightness and contrast, overall and per tonal range |
| Warmth, tint, vibrance, saturation | Take out a color cast, or push color further |
| Color wheels | Tint shadows, midtones and highlights separately |
| RGB curves | Redraw the brightness ramp — whole image, or red, green and blue one at a time |
| Hue curves | Pick one hue and move only it: shift, saturate or brighten |
| HSL selections | Key a band of hue, saturation and brightness, then correct only those pixels. Up to four, in order |
| Grain and vignette | Add texture, or darken the edges to pull the eye in |
| Custom LUT | Load a `.cube` file that maps every color to another |

The scopes measure the picture so you aren't judging by your screen: the **histogram** shows lost detail at either
end, the **waveform** shows where across the frame, the **RGB parade** names a color cast, and the **vectorscope**
puts skin tones on one known line.

**Copy grade to** reuses a grade on other clips, as a starting point; the same numbers rarely suit two shots.

## LUTs

A LUT (a `.cube` file, up to 65 points per side) maps every color to another, blended in at the strength you set.
Use creative Rec.709 LUTs. HyperFrames doesn't convert camera LOG footage first, so a LOG clip needs its camera's own
transform or comes out wrong.

## Limits

* An effect or grade covers the whole layer. It doesn't follow a face or an object: to treat part of the frame, put
  that part on its own layer.
* It applies to images, video and canvas, not to text or HTML.
* Standard video only. HDR sources preview in SDR and the effects don't carry into true HDR.
* Blur, Bloom and Kuwahara Paint are slow; several stacked on big layers slow preview and render.
* Keep media inside the project. A file on another server needs the right CORS headers and can vanish before render.

> [accordion] For agents and code: the commands and the stored format
>
> List what exists, measure a source, then apply. `--dry-run` shows the change, `--clear` removes it.
>
> ```bash theme={null}
> npx hyperframes media-treatment --capabilities --json
> npx hyperframes media-treatment --selector '#interview' --analyze --json
> npx hyperframes media-treatment --selector '#product' --grading '{"preset":"two-ink-print"}' --apply --json
> ```
>
> Compare several looks on one frame (up to sixteen, the original first):
>
> ```bash theme={null}
> npx hyperframes grade-compare --for frame.png --grades grades.json
> ```
>
> Phone photos keep their displayed orientation and aspect ratio in the sheet; the source image stays unchanged.
>
> Everything lands in `data-color-grading`, in named sections: `adjust` for corrections, `details` for grain and
> vignette, `effects` for treatments. A flat object such as `{"exposure":0.15}` renders nothing, and
> `npx hyperframes lint` says which section it belongs in.
>
> ```html theme={null}
> <video src="./interview.mp4" data-color-grading='{"preset":"skin-soft","intensity":0.7,"adjust":{"exposure":0.15},"effects":{"bloom":0.4}}'></video>
> ```
>
> The full format is in the [HTML schema](/reference/html-schema#color-grading-and-media-effects) and the
> [color grading reference](/reference/color-grading).

## Related topics

* [Use images and video](/guides/video-components)
* [Color, effects, 3D and generated art: the words to use](/prompting/color-grading)
* [Browse ready-made effects in the Catalog](/catalog)


# Motion Blur
Source: https://hyperframes.heygen.com/guides/motion-blur

Smear fast-moving elements along their path, in the browser editor preview and in renders. Off until you turn it on.

Motion blur gives fast-moving elements a real shutter smear. For each frame, HyperFrames reads where every mover was across the shutter interval and blurs it along that path. A box sliding across the frame leaves a streak instead of a sharp copy at one position.

It is **opt-in**. Nothing blurs until you add `data-motion-blur="on"` to the composition root.

## Turn it on

```html theme={null}
<div
  id="root"
  data-composition-id="main"
  data-width="1920"
  data-height="1080"
  data-duration="10"
  data-motion-blur="on"
>
  ...
</div>
```

That is all. The same attribute drives the browser editor preview and `hyperframes render`.

| Attribute | Default | Meaning |
| - | - | - |
| `data-motion-blur` | none | `on` enables blur. `off` opts out, on the root or on any subtree. |
| `data-motion-blur-shutter` | `240` | Shutter angle in degrees, 0–720. Larger is a longer smear. |
| `data-motion-blur-phase` | centred | When the shutter opens, in degrees of a frame, -360 to 360. The window starts at `t + phase / 360 / fps` and lasts `shutter / 360 / fps`. `0` opens on the frame, so the smear trails ahead of it; unset centres it, the same as minus half the shutter. Matches After Effects' Shutter Phase. |
| `data-motion-blur-samples` | at least 32 | A fixed number of samples per frame, 2–64. Left unset, each mover gets at least 32, and about one per 2 px of smear when that is more, so a fast move never shows steps. |
| `data-motion-blur-events` | off | `on` runs timeline callbacks (`onUpdate` and similar) while blur looks for movers, and at each sample when a callback changes an element's inline style or its box. Needed when the motion is set from a callback, such as a `render(t)` function, which blur cannot otherwise see. |
| `data-motion-blur-tier` | `auto` | `auto` and `filter` draw with the filter tier; `capture` asks for the capture tier (below). |

## In the browser editor

The **Blur** tab in the browser editor's right dock sets it with one control: **Off**, **Subtle** or **Strong**. Subtle is the default blur (240° shutter, samples sized to the smear). Strong opens the shutter to 720° and the samples to 64. The panel writes the attributes above to the composition root, so a render uses the same setting, and Undo works. Subtle and Strong also turn on `data-motion-blur-events`, so motion set from a `render(t)` callback is found. Off removes `data-motion-blur` and `data-motion-blur-events` and leaves the other attributes where they are.

## What it blurs

Elements that move quickly in 2D: position, scale and rotation changes from GSAP, CSS animations and transitions, and the Web Animations API. Slow movers and static content are left sharp. A mover's glow and shadow travel with it, and the background behind it stays where it is.

## Two ways it is drawn

**Filter** puts an SVG filter on each mover: copies of the element along its path, averaged, and softened along the motion. It is what `data-motion-blur-tier="auto"` (the default) draws with. It works in any Chrome and over a WebGL canvas. On a four-whip test it cost about what a render without blur costs; on two real films it cost more than capture (see Cost and limits). Turns and zooms are only softened, not streaked.

**Capture** is opt-in with `data-motion-blur-tier="capture"`. It copies each mover out of the page with Chrome's [HTML in Canvas](/guides/html-in-canvas) API and redraws it along its path. It draws turns and zooms truthfully: a spinning tile smears along its arc and its centre stays sharp, and a zoom streaks outward. It has limits of its own, listed here (the filter tier's are listed under Cost and limits, and a few, such as `backdrop-filter`, apply to both), so ask for it only for a film whose spins and zooms need the streak:

* Anything in front of a mover is lost: a static panel, an overlay or a title card over a moving element is drawn behind its smear.
* `mix-blend-mode` and `backdrop-filter` on a mover or its ancestor are not applied.
* A CSS selector that reaches the root through its parent, such as `body > #root > .m`, stops matching once capture wraps the root.
* A mover sliding into an `overflow: hidden` or clipped card drags the clip edge along, two overlapping movers carry each other's pixels, and content past the frame edge leaves a thin band.
* In preview, the first frame after every play shows black for a moment.

Capture needs a browser with HTML in Canvas. Chrome 157 and 158 builds exposed it without a flag in headless and Chrome-for-Testing builds; whether stable Chrome does is unverified. Chrome 155 and earlier need `chrome://flags/#html-in-canvas`.

A page that asks for capture gets the filter tier instead when capture cannot run:

| Found in the composition | Why capture cannot draw it |
| - | - |
| A WebGL or WebGPU canvas anywhere in the document | Captured frozen. |
| `backface-visibility: hidden` inside a 3D context (including from an animation) | Drawn mirrored. |
| A transform on the root element | Ignored by the capture. |
| Opacity below 1, or `mix-blend-mode`, on the root element | Not applied by the capture. |
| An `iframe`, `object`, `embed` or custom element in the root | Not captured faithfully. |
| A nested capture canvas, such as a VFX block | Hangs the renderer. |
| A browser without HTML in Canvas, or three failed captures in a row | Capture is unavailable. |

This is decided once for the whole composition, from the first frame. A defect the scan misses (a WebGL canvas added late, say) is caught per frame instead: that one frame is rendered sharp and counted in `failedFrames`.

Blur is off, and stays off, for HDR renders, distributed renders, and renders that use the engine's own sub-frame blur.

### Find out which one is drawing

```bash theme={null}
npx hyperframes check
```

| Finding | Severity | Meaning |
| - | - | - |
| `motion_blur_filter_fallback` | info | The page asked for capture, which could not run, so the filter tier draws. The message names the cause. |
| `motion_blur_no_movers` | info | Blur is on but nothing moves fast enough to blur. If the motion is set from a callback, add `data-motion-blur-events="on"`. |
| `motion_blur_unverified` | info | The page asks for capture and the check browser cannot run it, so it drew with the filter tier. Render once to see capture. |

In the page, `window.__hfMotionBlur.report()` returns `state`, `tier`, `reason`, `reasonCode` and `movers`. A render logs one line per session with the tier, and a session-end line when any frames fell back to sharp (`failedFrames > 0`).

## Cost and limits

* **Render time.** It varies by film. On an 8 s test composition with four whips, a render took 9.8 s with capture, 5.2–5.4 s with the filter tier and 5.3–5.9 s with no blur (two runs each, including startup). On two real 1080p films the filter tier cost more than capture, measured as CPU seconds of the whole render (wall time was too noisy on a loaded machine): `spacex-launch` (77 movers, 39.5 s) took 547–552 CPU s with the filter tier, 302–320 with capture and 184–193 with no blur (three runs each, 2.9 times no blur); `k3-promo` (106 movers, 16.5 s) took 236, 205 and 117 (one run per arm, 2.0 times no blur). The two films do not order by mover count, and the cause of the difference was not isolated. The filter tier draws each mover as at least 32 offset copies per frame; capture adds a second paint per blurred frame.
* **Editing.** The filter tier never wraps anything. With capture the root is wrapped only while playing or rendering; paused, it is plain DOM, so click-to-select works.
* **Capture only.** Blurred preview can run at half the frame rate on heavy compositions, and a `<video>` drawn through the capture looks about 2–3% darker in the browser editor preview than in normal playback. Renders are not affected.
* **Preview and render.** `auto` draws the same way in both. A page that asks for capture previews with the filter tier in a browser without HTML in Canvas, so a spin or zoom looks softer there than in the render.
* **Worker count.** Output is not bit-identical between worker counts (around 60 dB PSNR), about the size of the difference chunking already causes.
* **Not handled.** Pose errors under CSS `zoom`, `position: fixed` and `foreignObject`; a very short Web Animations API animation that falls between scan samples; a large see-through mover (a full-frame translucent sweep), which is left sharp while its fast children still blur. With capture, a mover is drawn above the static content, so a static element that should cover a mover does not.
* **Limits of the filter tier** (the default), as measured on one-pattern test compositions:
  * `::before` or `::after` content outside the mover's box is cut off.
  * A mover's own `clip-path` or mask gets hard edges: the smear is clipped to the shape it has at that frame.
  * A `position: fixed` child of a mover that moves via `left` jumps, because the filter makes the mover its containing block.
  * A `:last-child` selector on the root's children also matches the `<svg>` the tier adds to the root (`nth-last-*` works the same way but was not measured).
  * A visibility toggle inside the shutter window is drawn at full strength instead of half.
  * `backdrop-filter` on a mover differs from the 32-sample oracle in the sweep (the backdrop only).


# Make motion graphics with AI
Source: https://hyperframes.heygen.com/guides/motion-graphics

Make a short, motion-led title, statistic, chart, logo sting, or overlay.

Make a motion graphic for one short, design-led idea—usually under ten seconds—where the movement carries the message.

<video aria-label="Kinetic type, a count-up, a chart, a logo sting, a lower third" />

Short beats back to back, because that is what a motion graphic is — units of
motion small enough to drop into something else.

## Make it

**Point at a motion you like.** Under **Remix from inspiration** on Home, **Motion graphics** holds short moments
from real videos: choose **Add as inspiration** on one and say what yours should say. A link to any clip works
too, in **Make something** or under **Reference**.

**Or describe it** in a sentence:

```text theme={null}
A six-second motion graphic that counts from zero to 10,000 and lands on "Thank you." No narration.
```

Say whether you want a finished video or a transparent overlay when it could be either. With your own agent instead of the app, start the message with `/hyperframes`.

## What are you animating?

* **Words** — use kinetic type when movement and emphasis carry the message.
* **One number** — count or reveal a statistic, settle on the result, and hold it long enough to register.
* **Data** — animate a chart or comparison so the sequence makes the conclusion clear.
* **Logo** — build a short sting with a deliberate entrance, completion, and clean hold.
* **Overlay** — create a lower third or callout that enters, holds, and clears completely over footage.
* **Page, post, or map** — capture the real source and animate one detail into the visual payoff.

The same request shape can animate kinetic type, a statistic, chart, logo, lower third, map, real webpage, news headline, or post.

If the result needs narration, several scenes, or a longer story, make a [custom video](/guides/general-video).

> [card] [Practice it: A quick win: animate your logo](https://hyperframes.heygen.com/lessons/logo-quick-win)
>
> Free 18-minute lesson with a short video, a quiz and a brief to try. A short brief is enough: how long, what shape, your logo file and any words in quotes.

## Choose the output

* **MP4** for a finished standalone graphic.
* **WebM or MOV with transparency** for a logo sting, lower third, callout, or other overlay placed over footage.

For an overlay, name where it should sit and how long it should hold. The first and final frames must clear cleanly.

## Prompts that work

The canonical shape: routed, spec'd, beat-timestamped, copy quoted, technique pinned, gaps closed.

> Make an 8-second 1920x1080 video. Beat 1 (0-4s): dark macOS terminal types "npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes" character by character, then hold on the blinking cursor. Beat 2 (4-5s): the terminal shatters into fragments. Beat 3 (5-8s): bold white kinetic text on black slams in word by word, snappy: "YOU JUST MADE THIS / WITH HYPERFRAMES." Adapt the `code-typing` and `vfx-shatter` registry blocks; hand-author the kinetic text. No narration, no image or media files.

<video aria-label="Validate anatomy terminal" />

*Made from the prompt above.*

### Say these when they matter

**Duration.** Keep it short — motion graphics live under 10 seconds, up to \~30. A 2-second idea stretched to 8 feels slow no matter how it's animated; if the piece genuinely needs multiple scenes or a longer runtime, it's a multi-scene video, not a motion graphic.

**MP4 vs transparent overlay.** The default output is an MP4. Ask for a transparent overlay — a lower-third, a callout, a bug meant to composite over other footage — and the render targets `webm` or `mov` with alpha. Transparency only makes sense when part of the frame is *meant* to be empty. A full-frame design (its own background, edge-to-edge composition) has nothing to be transparent, so asking for a transparent WebM there produces either an opaque file or a broken-looking one. Say "transparent overlay, alpha channel" only for pieces designed to sit on top of something else.

**Registry blocks vs freeform.** Naming a block (`apple-money-count`, `x-post`, `data-chart`, `code-typing`, `us-map` / `world-map`) makes the agent compose reuse-first: install the block, customize in place, hand-author only the gaps. Omit the block and it hand-builds from your description — fine for one-off looks, more drift on the details you didn't pin. Name blocks exactly as they appear in the [catalog](/catalog/blocks/data-chart).

**Easing and motion feel.** The words you use for *how* motion feels — "snappy", "bouncy", "settles with overshoot" — map to specific eases. Spend them; they're cheap precision. See [Vocabulary](/prompting/motion#words-for-how-motion-feels) for the adjective-to-ease table and [Premium motion](/prompting/motion) for the grammar that keeps a piece from reading cheap (nothing fully stops, action overlaps, the camera acts).

### Variants

Each reuses a registry block, so the agent composes rather than hand-building from scratch.

> [accordion] Stat count-up
>
> > 6-second 1920x1080 video, dark navy background. Beat 1 (0-1s): label "ARR" fades up small, top-center. Beat 2 (1-4s): a giant number counts up to \$4.2M with an odometer roll, easing out as it lands. Beat 3 (4-6s): "+312% YoY" stamps in below in green, then everything settles into a gentle ambient idle (subtle breathing scale, slow particle drift). Use the `apple-money-count` registry block as base. No narration.

> [accordion] Logo sting
>
> > 5-second 1920x1080 logo sting. Beat 1 (0-2s): the word "ACME" assembles from scattered particles. Beat 2 (2-3s): full-frame `swirl-vortex` shader transition. Beat 3 (3-5s): logo lockup + tagline "Ship faster." settles on white, then holds with a subtle ambient idle (slow breathing scale). Use `code-particle-assemble` for the assembly.

> [accordion] Animated tweet
>
> > 7-second 1080x1350 vertical video. A real tweet card (handle @hyperframes, text "we render video from HTML now. no timeline UI. just code.") slides up over a soft animated gradient, likes counter ticks 0→1.2K, then the card tilts in 3D and a highlight sweeps the second sentence. Settle into a gentle ambient idle on the card at the end. Use the `x-post` and `vfx-liquid-background` registry blocks. No narration, no image or media files.

> [accordion] Map route
>
> > 8-second 1920x1080 video. Dark world map, a glowing arc animates from San Francisco to Tokyo over 3s, destination pin drops with a pulse, then camera zooms into Tokyo and the label "LATENCY: 89ms" types on. Use the `nyc-paris-flight` registry block as the base pattern, restyle to teal on charcoal. No narration.

### Common mistakes

**Transparent output on a full-frame design.** Alpha is for overlay elements, not for pieces that fill the frame. A design with its own background has no transparent region to export.

* **Avoid:** `an 8s full-screen stat count-up on dark navy — export as a transparent WebM`
* **Instead:** `an 8s stat count-up on dark navy, MP4` — or, for a bug to composite over footage: `just the count-up chip, no background, transparent overlay (webm)`

**Narration on a motion-is-the-message piece.** Motion graphics are unnarrated by definition — the visual carries it. A voice-over makes it a narrated video.

* **Avoid:** `a 10s logo sting with a voice-over reading the tagline`
* **Instead:** `a 10s logo sting, no narration` — for a spoken track, ask for a narrated explainer instead.

**Stretching a short idea long.** Runtime is a knob, and past \~30s a single motion beat runs out of things to do.

* **Avoid:** `a 45-second kinetic-type piece of one headline`
* **Instead:** `an 8-second kinetic-type piece of one headline` — or promote it to a multi-scene video.

> [!TIP]
>
> For the six-part skeleton and the per-beat content formula these prompts share, see [Prompt anatomy](/prompting/overview#the-shape-of-a-strong-prompt); for the full set of run-verified examples, [Verified examples](/prompting/examples).

## Review the motion

* The words, data, source, and logo are exact.
* The complete message is readable while the video plays.
* The main movement helps communicate the meaning.
* The opening and ending states are deliberate.
* A transparent export has been checked over real footage.

> [card] [Finish and share](/guides/export-and-share)
>
> Check the motion at full speed, render the chosen format, and review the final file.

## A finished one, end to end

The demo above shows the range. This is a complete graphic built from it —
music and sound, no narration, the motion carrying all of it.

<video aria-label="A complete year-in-review motion graphic" />

A complete year-in-review graphic. It uses music and sound, but no narration; the motion carries it.

# Make a music video or lyric video
Source: https://hyperframes.heygen.com/guides/music-to-video

Cut footage, images, lyrics, and motion to a track’s beat grid.

Start with a music file—or a video whose audio should control the edit. Narration is not added; the track is the spine.

<video aria-label="A complete music-driven film" />

A complete music-driven film. Its sections, visual treatments, and cuts follow the track.

## Make it

Add the track (and any photos or clips that must appear) in **Make something**:

```text theme={null}
Turn this song and the tour photos into a 30-second video cut to the beat.
```

**Have an edit you like?** Paste its link too and say "cut it like this": the agent matches its rhythm and
transitions to your track. Mention a section, lyric or image order only when it can't be chosen freely. With your own agent instead of the app, start the message with `/hyperframes`.

## What should the track drive?

* **Use your photos or video** — cut approved media to the track's phrases, energy, beats, and ending.
* **Make a lyric video** — verify the words first, then synchronize and design each line around the vocal.
* **Invent the visuals** — build the visual arc from typography, graphic elements, and motion when no media is supplied.

A complete video can also be built entirely from type, graphic templates, and
motion.

## The track sets the structure

HyperFrames maps the track’s phrases, energy, onsets, silences, rolls, drops, and hard stops before it plans the visuals.

A rhythmic track can support cuts on its real beat grid. Calm or loose music should flow by phrase and energy instead of forcing a cut onto every measured beat.

The visual treatments change at meaningful musical moments. More beats do not automatically mean more scenes.

## Prompts that work

The verified starting point: photos cut to a track, exported to a square MP4.

> 20-second 1080x1080 video from ./track.mp3 (pick the best 20 seconds of the track) and the 8 photos in ./shots/. Cut on the beat grid, one photo per bar, punch-in on downbeats, `whip-pan` transitions on phrase changes. End on the last photo with "SUMMER '26" in condensed caps. No TTS.

<video aria-label="Example music slideshow" />

*Made from the prompt above.*

Every timing decision here is delegated to the track's own analysis — you describe the *treatment* ("one photo per bar", "punch-in on downbeats"), and the beat grid supplies the *times*.

### Say these when they matter

**The beat grid.** The agent analyzes the track (`hyperframes beats`, `hyperframes audio`) for beats, onsets, and sections, then cuts at real musical changes. You steer *how* it cuts, not *when*: "one photo per bar" sets cut density, "punch-in on downbeats" adds the accent, "transitions on phrase changes" reserves the visible moves for structural boundaries. On genuinely rhythmic music the grid is trustworthy and cuts snap to the beat; on calm music the grid is a metronome the analyzer imposed, so the agent paces by phrase and energy instead of hard-cutting — say "let it flow, no hard cuts" if the track is ambient.

**Track section — describe, don't timestamp.** Ask for "the best 20 seconds" or "the verse into the hook" and let the analyzer choose boundaries that land on musical anchors. Hard timestamps ("use 0:32–0:52") cut mid-phrase and fight the grid.

**Asset supply.** Zero assets is valid — typography carries a complete video. Any photos or clips you hand it are woven in *on the same beat grid* (beat-cut or Ken Burns), so more assets means more to cut between, not a different pacing model. Point at a directory ("the 8 photos in ./shots/") and name the end card.

### Variants

> [accordion] Lyric video
>
> > 30-second 1080x1920 lyric video from ./song.mp3 (pick the strongest 30-second section — a verse into the hook). Transcribe the vocals for word timing. Lines rise in one at a time on the beat, big condensed type on a dark grain background; the hook lands with each word punching in on its downbeat. Keyword in each line highlighted in acid green. No photos — typography only. No TTS.
>
> Word-level timing comes from transcribing the track (or from lyrics you paste, placed on the beat grid). No supplied assets needed — type is the whole video.

> [accordion] Kinetic promo from a mood brief (no track)
>
> > 15-second 1080x1080 kinetic promo. No track supplied — generate one: driving synthwave, high energy. Cut hard on the beat: full-frame word cards ("FASTER", "SHARPER", "SHIP IT") slam in on downbeats, alternating black/white with inverted type, a glitch flash on each phrase change. End on the wordmark "NOVA" holding with a subtle ambient idle. No TTS.
>
> With no audio supplied, the track is generated from the mood you describe; the beat grid it produces still drives every cut.

### Common mistakes

**Hard track timestamps.** The whole point of a music video is that the track's structure sets the cuts. A literal time window ignores the analyzed beat grid and lands cuts mid-phrase.

* **Avoid:** `use the section from 0:32 to 0:52`
* **Instead:** `pick the best 20 seconds of the track`

**Expecting an MP4 from a presentation.** A presentation is a live deck you click through; it doesn't export as one video file.

* **Avoid:** `a slideshow deck, then render it to MP4`
* **Instead:** `a music video from these photos` for a file to post, or `a presentation` to click through live

**Wrong deliverable for the output.** Photos set to music that you'll export and post is a video; a thing you click through live is a presentation. Picking by the word "slideshow" alone builds the wrong deliverable.

> [!TIP]
>
> The music prompts here are unnarrated; ask for a voice-over if you want one. For the six-part skeleton these prompts share, see [Prompt anatomy](/prompting/overview#the-shape-of-a-strong-prompt); for adjectives that map to eases and transitions, [Vocabulary](/prompting/motion#words-for-how-motion-feels).

A clause from a longer film prompt that makes the cuts follow the real beats, ready to lift:

> **Rhythm (45–52s).** The wire becomes a waveform: **resolve the BGM first, run `hyperframes beats` on it, and drive this region on the detected grid** — the waveform pulses and compact media cards (a lyric line, a photo card, a chart flash) snap onto the wire on real analyzed beats while the camera keeps traveling; each snap gets a tick SFX. At least six beat-hits. SANCTIONED SEAM #2: the beat-hits may hard-cut card content ON the beat — the sanctioned exception, because the camera itself never stops moving through them.

<video aria-label="Capstone region rhythm" />

*Cuts landing on the detected beats of a real track (`npx hyperframes beats`).*

## Review the rhythm

* The correct section of the track is used.
* Required media appears and lyrics match the vocal.
* The strongest visual changes land on meaningful musical changes.
* Important images and text remain long enough to understand.
* The ending reaches a musical landing or forms a deliberate loop.

For direct timing control, use the [browser editor timeline](/studio/timeline) to refine
cuts, holds, and the ending against the beat markers. Ask the agent when the
section, media plan, or overall treatment must change.

> [card] [Finish and share](/guides/export-and-share)
>
> Check the final project, render through your preferred surface, and review the file.

## Related topics

* [Edit cuts and holds on the browser editor timeline](/studio/timeline)
* [Work with voice, music, sound, and captions](/guides/voice-and-audio)


# Fix a slow preview or render
Source: https://hyperframes.heygen.com/guides/performance

Find the expensive part of a composition and make it cheaper.

A finished render can be smooth even when preview stutters. Preview must draw each frame in real time; render can take as long as it needs to capture the same frames.

<video aria-label="The same composition built two ways, timed on this machine" />

Real numbers, not estimates: 25.0s against 9.8s, taken as the median of three
runs at 1920x1080 over 300 frames. One CSS declaration is the whole difference,
and a pixel comparison confirms the picture did not change.

## Start with the symptom

| What you see | Check first |
| - | - |
| Preview stutters in one scene | Large blurs, masks, shadows, or many animated layers in that scene |
| Preview pauses the first time an image appears | Oversized source images or image decoding |
| The whole page becomes slow | Script work, layout thrashing, or too many DOM nodes |
| Render is slow but the result is correct | Source-video extraction, frame capture, or encoding |
| WebM takes much longer than MP4 | VP9 encoding; transparent WebM is CPU-heavy |

## Reduce expensive browser work

* Use fewer large `backdrop-filter` and `filter: blur()` layers.
* Avoid animating dozens of shadowed elements at once.
* Replace a static blur or texture stack with a pre-rendered image.
* Size images near their actual delivery dimensions. A very large JPEG still decodes into a very large bitmap.
* Keep work inside animation callbacks small. Do not repeatedly read layout and write styles in the same frame.

For a 1920×1080 composition, a 3840×2160 source already provides enough detail for a 2× display. Larger sources usually add memory and decode work without improving the frame.

## Measure instead of guessing

1. Run `npx hyperframes preview`.
2. Open Chrome DevTools and select **Performance**.
3. Record the part that stutters.
4. Inspect the longest tasks:
   * **Paint** or **Composite Layers** points to filters, shadows, masks, or large layers.
   * **Layout** or **Recalculate Style** points to layout work.
   * **Script** points to author code.

Change one expensive feature, record again, and keep the version that moves the bottleneck.

## Make a fast review render

If the composition is intentionally too heavy for real-time playback, review an encoded file:

```bash theme={null}
npx hyperframes render --quality draft --output review.mp4
```

Use `standard` or `high` for delivery. Draft changes capture and encoder quality; it does not change the composition's timing.

## Tune transparent WebM only when needed

WebM uses the CPU-heavy VP9 encoder. The default is suitable for most work. To trade more encoding time for compression quality:

```bash theme={null}
npx hyperframes render --format webm --vp9-cpu-used 2 --output overlay.webm
```

`--vp9-cpu-used` accepts integers from `-8` to `8`; higher values are faster with a larger quality/size tradeoff.

## Related topics

* [Diagnose a failed or stalled render](/help)
* [Render from the command line](/guides/rendering)
* [Render at 4K](/guides/4k-rendering)


# Install the HyperFrames plugin
Source: https://hyperframes.heygen.com/guides/plugins

Install video creation skills as one versioned plugin and let your agent manage updates.

The HyperFrames plugin gives your coding agent every HyperFrames skill: the video
contract and references for product promos, explainers, captions, motion graphics,
and more, plus the CLI, registry, and media skills. Skills load when needed.

Choose one installation method per agent. Plugins receive updates through the
agent's plugin manager. [Standalone skills](/guides/skills) remain available for
OpenCode and other agents, or when you prefer the smaller core-only install.

| Agent | Installation route |
| - | - |
| Claude Code | HyperFrames' GitHub marketplace |
| Copilot CLI | HyperFrames' GitHub marketplace |
| VS Code / Copilot | Add the GitHub marketplace in the Extensions view |
| Cursor | Import through a team marketplace, or load a local plugin |
| Gemini CLI | Install the HyperFrames extension from GitHub |
| Codex | Use your existing HyperFrames plugin; directory updates are published separately |
| OpenCode | Use standalone skills |

You need Node.js 22+ and npm for the local CLI, plus FFmpeg for rendering.
Install on each machine you use; a plugin does not synchronize your machines.

## Claude Code

Run in your terminal:

```bash theme={null}
claude plugin marketplace add heygen-com/hyperframes
claude plugin install hyperframes@hyperframes
claude plugin details hyperframes
```

The inventory should include `hyperframes`, `hyperframes-cli`, and `media-use`.
Start a new session or run `/reload-plugins`, then try:

```text theme={null}
Using /hyperframes:hyperframes, make a 5-second title card that says "Hello world".
```

**Enable automatic updates in Claude Code's terminal UI:** open a terminal in
your project and run `claude`. In that session, run `/plugin`, open **Marketplaces**,
select **hyperframes**, and choose **Enable auto-update**. If you installed through
Claude Code's IDE extension or desktop app, use this terminal route on the same
machine. Third-party marketplaces do not enable this by default. See
[Claude Code's auto-update guidance](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/install#turn-auto-update-on-or-off-for-a-marketplace)
for details. To update manually:

```bash theme={null}
claude plugin update hyperframes@hyperframes
```

Reload plugins after updating. To remove the plugin:

```bash theme={null}
claude plugin uninstall hyperframes@hyperframes
```

See [Claude's plugin guide](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/install)
for project-wide installation and managed update policies.

## GitHub Copilot CLI

```bash theme={null}
copilot plugin marketplace add heygen-com/hyperframes
copilot plugin install hyperframes@hyperframes
copilot plugin list
```

Start a fresh session and ask Copilot to use the HyperFrames skill to make the
same title card. Check `/skills list` if the skill is not visible.

```bash theme={null}
copilot plugin update hyperframes
copilot plugin uninstall hyperframes
```

These are explicit updates; do not assume Copilot CLI shares VS Code's update
schedule. See [Copilot's plugin guide](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/customize-copilot/plugins-finding-installing).

## VS Code

Open the Extensions view and search `@agentPlugins`. Add
`heygen-com/hyperframes` as a marketplace using the plugin marketplace command,
then install **hyperframes** and verify its skills in Agent Customizations.
Agent plugins must be enabled in VS Code settings.

VS Code checks for updates every 24 hours when `extensions.autoUpdate` is enabled.
Use **Extensions: Check for Extension Updates** for a manual check. Disable or
uninstall the plugin from the Extensions view. See [VS Code's plugin guide](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agent-customization/agent-plugins)
for the current UI and workspace recommendations.

## Cursor

For a team marketplace, import `heygen-com/hyperframes` in **Dashboard → Plugins &
MCPs** and add the HyperFrames plugin. Teammates install it from **Customize**.
GitHub marketplace auto-refresh requires the Cursor GitHub App and the marketplace's
**Enable Auto Refresh** setting.

For a local install, copy an extracted HyperFrames plugin folder to
`~/.cursor/plugins/local/hyperframes`, then reload Cursor and check **Customize**.
The folder must contain `plugin.json` and `skills/`. Local copies require manual
replacement to update; they do not subscribe to GitHub changes. Enterprise policy
may disable local plugin imports. Remove the local folder to uninstall that copy.

This repository's manifests are not proof of a public Cursor marketplace listing.
Public listings and their updates go through Cursor review. See [Cursor's plugin
guide](https://cursor.com/docs/plugins) for marketplace and local-install controls.

## Gemini CLI

```bash theme={null}
gemini extensions install https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes --auto-update
gemini extensions list
```

Restart Gemini CLI and ask it to use the HyperFrames skill for the title card.
To manage the extension explicitly:

```bash theme={null}
gemini extensions update hyperframes
gemini extensions uninstall hyperframes
```

To stay on a specific release, install with `--ref <release-tag>` instead of
`--auto-update`. Choose a release containing `gemini-extension.json`.
See [Gemini's extension guide](https://geminicli.com/docs/extensions/reference/).

The plugin itself remains read-only and does not include browsers or model
weights.

## Versions and updates

The plugin bundles workflows from one source snapshot and runs the CLI version
recorded in its manifest. Your agent should use its bundled plugin launcher;
it should not run `npx hyperframes skills update` during a plugin workflow.
Existing project dependencies, downloaded media, and external services have their
own versions and are not frozen by the plugin.

Update behavior depends on the client and source ref. For example,
[Cursor GitHub Auto Refresh](https://cursor.com/docs/plugins#keep-plugins-up-to-date)
follows pushes to the tracked branch, so skill content can change without a new
CLI version. The manifest pins the CLI version, not the installed skill commit.
For a repeatable installation, keep a release tag or an extracted release archive
and disable automatic updates. Install that same release on each machine.
Git-based installs may download the full source repository. Release ZIPs contain
only the plugin payload, but loading an extracted ZIP locally requires manual updates.
Only releases with a `hyperframes-agent-plugin.zip` asset provide that portable ZIP.

## Move from standalone skills or core-skills

Install the full plugin and verify its inventory first. In Claude, an older
`core-skills@hyperframes` install can then be removed:

```bash theme={null}
claude plugin uninstall core-skills@hyperframes
```

Use your standalone skill manager to remove only the old HyperFrames skills for
that agent. Inspect the locations first: other agents may share a global skills
store, and locally edited skills should be backed up. Do not delete an entire
`.agents` or `.claude` directory. Restart the agent and confirm it selects the
plugin copy rather than a duplicate standalone skill.

## If a workflow is missing or stale

1. Check the agent's installed plugin inventory and version.
2. Update using that agent's plugin manager, then reload or restart it.
3. Check whether an old standalone installation is also being loaded.
4. For a pinned release, verify the workflow exists in that release. Do not mix
   skills from a newer release into the plugin folder.

## Related topics

* [Make your first video](/quickstart)
* [Install standalone skills](/guides/skills)
* [Plugin release checklist](/contributing/agent-plugins)


# Turn a GitHub PR into a video
Source: https://hyperframes.heygen.com/guides/pr-to-video

Paste a pull request link and get a short video of what changed and why it matters, for users, reviewers or social.

Give it a pull request link. The agent reads the diff, the commits and who worked on it, then explains the change.

<video aria-label="A pull request explained with code and before-and-after behavior" />

*A real pull request as a 32-second explanation: code, before and after, and sound.*

## Make it

Paste the pull request link into **Make something** and say who will watch:

```text theme={null}
Explain https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/123 to product and engineering teammates.
```

The agent reads the actual pull request and checks whether it has shipped, so a proposed change is never shown as
released. If your team already has a release video you like, add its link and ask for the same style. With your own agent instead of the app, start the message with `/hyperframes`.

## Pick the story for the audience

* **Users:** lead with the visible change, show before and after, name any action they must take.
* **Contributors:** the architecture change, the tradeoff, the code path a reviewer needs.
* **Social:** one feature reveal with visible proof and only the code that explains it.

Say whether it's a changelog, a feature reveal, a fix or a refactor, and mention any breaking change. The video
explains the change; it doesn't read the description aloud.

## Prompts that work

Verified, from the [examples](/prompting/examples) page — a 30-second feature reveal:

> Make a 30-second 1920x1080 feature-reveal video from \[PR URL]. Lead with what users get, not the diff; show the key code change with the `code-diff` block for one beat only; end on version number + repo URL. No narration, kinetic captions instead.

<video aria-label="Example PR video" />

*Made from the prompt above.*

### Say these when they matter

| Knob | What to say | Why it matters |
| - | - | - |
| **Impact vs diff** | "lead with what users get, not the diff" | The video explains the *change*, it doesn't read the diff aloud; opening on impact answers "why should I care?" before the code |
| **How many hunks** | "one `code-diff` beat only" / "at most two hunks" | Code beats feature 2-4 real hunks total, each a small legible snippet — a whole file is unreadable at video scale |
| **Which code block** | `code-diff` for a delta · `code-morph` for a refactor · `code-typing` for new code | The block matches the story: a diff shows added/removed lines, a morph shows one shape becoming another |
| **Angle** | "changelog" / "feature-reveal" / "fix-explainer" / "refactor-walkthrough" | Sets the story shape; the agent reshapes the PR into it rather than walking files in diff order |
| **Audience** | "for developers" (default) / "mixed technical" / "non-technical stakeholders" | Shifts how much the narration assumes — a non-technical cut leans harder on impact and lighter on code |
| **End card** | "end on version number + repo URL" | The conventional close for a code explainer; state what goes on it so it's a real CTA, not an afterthought |
| **Narration vs captions** | "calm male narration" or "no narration, kinetic captions instead" | Both are supported; captions-only keeps it silent-friendly for social, narration carries a longer walkthrough |
| **Length** | "\~30s" for one headline, up to \~3 min for a large PR | The agent sizes the video from the change — a huge PR is a ceiling on story, not a floor to fill |

### Variants

> [accordion] Changelog roundup
>
> > Make a \~40-second 1920x1080 changelog video from \[PR URL]. Changelog angle: open with the release line, then one beat per notable change — a short label and a one-line "what it does" each. Show at most two `code-diff` hunks across the whole video. End on version + repo URL. Calm male TTS narration, no captions.
>
> <video aria-label="Variant PR changelog" />
>
> *Rendered from this prompt with \[PR URL] = heygen-com/hyperframes#2092, unedited.*
>
> A changelog trades depth for breadth — many small changes, each a beat, rather than one change explored deeply. Keep code beats sparse so the pace stays fast. A PR doesn't carry its shipping version — the agent finds it from the release tag or the package manifest on main.

> [accordion] Fix explainer
>
> > Make a \~40-second 1920x1080 fix-explainer from \[PR URL], for developers. Fix angle: state the bug's symptom first, then the root cause, then the one-line fix on the `code-diff` block. End on version + repo URL. No narration, kinetic captions.
>
> A fix reads as symptom → cause → fix. Lead with what users saw break, not the stack trace — the diff is the payoff, not the opening.

> [accordion] Refactor walkthrough
>
> > Make a \~70-second 1920x1080 refactor-walkthrough from \[PR URL], for developers. Refactor angle: why the old shape hurt, then the new shape, showing the before/after with the `code-morph` block for the key file. End on version + repo URL. Calm male TTS narration.
>
> A refactor changes shape without changing behavior, so the story is *why* the new structure is better. `code-morph` animates one form transforming into another — the right block when the point is the transition, not a line-by-line delta.

### Common mistakes

**Asking for the whole diff.** A PR video explains the change; it doesn't recite every file. A full diff is unreadable at video scale.

* **Avoid:** `walk through the entire diff, file by file`
* **Instead:** `feature the 2-3 key hunks, each a small legible snippet`

**Opening on the code.** The diff is the payoff, not the hook — lead with what the change means.

* **Avoid:** `start with the diff, then explain what it does`
* **Instead:** `lead with what users get, then show the key hunk`

**Hard-timing a narrated cut.** The spoken length sets the runtime, so give a range.

* **Avoid:** `a 40-second narrated walkthrough`
* **Instead:** `a ~40-second narrated walkthrough`

## Verify the proof

* The pull request and target branch are correct.
* Proposed, merged, and released are not confused.
* User-facing claims match the actual behavior.
* Code excerpts show only the relevant lines and remain readable.
* Tests and refactoring are not presented as product features.
* Contributor names and release details are accurate.

Ask the agent when the explanation or the evidence must change; fix a timing, a code crop or a caption by hand in
the editor.

## Related topics

* [Create a custom video from several sources](/guides/general-video)


# Make a product launch video with AI
Source: https://hyperframes.heygen.com/guides/product-launch-video

Paste your product's URL and get a launch video built from its real screens, colors and words. Then change anything.

Paste your product's URL and you get a launch video built from what's really there: its screens, colors, fonts and
words. HyperFrames is free, and a launch video takes the agent about 10 to 15 minutes to build.

<video aria-label="A launch film built from huly.io, end to end" />

Built from huly.io. The screens are captured from the real site, not mocked.

## Make it

**In the Studio app**, paste the URL into **Make something** with one line about the video, and choose **Let's go**.
Turn on **Start with a storyboard** to approve the shots as stills before anything moves.

```text theme={null}
A 30-second launch video for https://example.com.
```

**Seen a launch you'd love to copy?** Open **Reference** on Home, paste its link (or pick one under **Pick a
reference**), and add your URL: you get that structure and energy with your product in it. Reference uses your
HeyGen API key, and the app asks for it the first time.

Add only what must be exact: the audience, a claim, the final action. Say **don't capture the website** when the
video should use only your brief. With your own agent instead of the app, start the message with `/hyperframes`.

## Pick the kind

* **Launch video**: the product's real evidence arranged into a story with one clear action at the end.
* **Product tour**: one complete task through the real screens, from the first click to the result.
* **Short social video**: one useful point, its proof, then stop.

No product to show? Make a [faceless explainer](/guides/faceless-explainer) instead.

## Prompts that work

When you want to set the structure, voice and music yourself:

> Make a 45-second 1920x1080 launch video for [https://linear.app](https://linear.app). Energetic but minimal, use the site's own palette and screenshots. Structure: hook stating the problem, 3 feature beats with UI captures and one-line captions, end card with logo + "Try it free". Female TTS voice, confident tone, subtle electronic BGM under -18dB.

<video aria-label="Example product launch" />

*A launch film made from this prompt.*

### Say these when they matter

Set the ones you care about and leave the rest to the agent.

| Knob | What to say | Why it matters |
| - | - | - |
| **Capture vs no capture** | Give a URL to capture the real site; give a script or brief when there is no site to capture | Capture borrows the real palette and screenshots; without it the visuals are invented, so name your brand colors |
| **Palette source** | "use the site's own palette" | The agent builds from the captured brand tokens — you get the product's real colors, not a generic theme |
| **Structure** | "hook stating the problem, N feature beats with captions, end card with CTA" | Naming the beats keeps the hook and CTA from getting dropped |
| **Voice & tone** | "female TTS voice, confident" / "calm male voice" | Voice gender and tone are prompt words; the provider itself is the agent's decision — see [media and audio](/prompting/media-and-audio) for provider mechanics |
| **BGM level** | "subtle electronic BGM under -18dB" (or "no BGM") | A stated ceiling keeps music under the voice; leave it off entirely for a teaser |
| **Length & destination** | "\~45 seconds", "9:16 for TikTok" | Sweet spot is 30-90s; destination sets the aspect (16:9 embed · 1:1 feed · 9:16 Shorts) |

> [!TIP]
>
> Duration and destination are the two cheapest, highest-leverage things to state. Everything else the agent will choose well if you stay quiet — see [the specification dial](/prompting/overview#how-much-to-specify) for how much to delegate.

### Variants

> [accordion] 20-second vertical teaser (9:16)
>
> > Make a \~20-second 1080x1920 teaser for [https://linear.app](https://linear.app). Super minimal, just the hook. Beat 1 (0-4s): the problem in one line, big type. Beat 2 (4-16s): two feature beats, one UI capture each with a three-word caption. Beat 3 (16-20s): logo + "Try it free" end card, held still to the end. Use the site's own palette. Female TTS voice, confident; no BGM.
>
> A teaser trades feature coverage for pace — fewer beats, one idea each. Keep the destination (Shorts / TikTok → 9:16) and let the agent scale the story to the shorter runtime.

> [accordion] Pasted script, no capture
>
> > Make a \~20-second 1920x1080 launch video from this script — use it verbatim: "Your CRM is three hours of busywork a day. AutoCRM logs every call, email, and meeting for you. 200 teams already switched. Try it free at autocrmhq.com." No site to capture — invent clean product-y visuals from the script. Male TTS voice, calm and confident; subtle BGM under -18dB.
>
> With no URL there is nothing to capture: no screenshots, no site palette to borrow, so name your brand colors and fonts if you have them (or the agent invents a palette). Verbatim scripts set the duration — figure roughly 130 spoken words per minute, so a 30-second video wants a 65–70 word script. Saying "use it verbatim" settles whether the agent may restructure your words.

> [accordion] Site tour instead (same URL, tour brief)
>
> > Make a 30-second 1920x1080 tour of [https://example.com](https://example.com) built from its own screenshots. Calm, editorial pace — show the homepage, two inner pages, and the footer. Full narration, warm male voice. This is a showcase, not a sales pitch.
>
> Reach for this when the goal is to *show the site*, not sell a product. It builds from captured screenshots and the site's brand assets. A launch or promo from the same URL is a different brief — ask to sell it.

### Common mistakes

**Hard-timing a verbatim script.** With supplied narration, the real TTS duration sets the length — a hard number forces the agent to cut or pad your words.

* **Avoid:** `a 45-second launch video from this exact script: ...`
* **Instead:** `a ~45-second launch video from this script: ...`

**Dropping the structure.** Hook → value → evidence → CTA is there for a reason; drop the hook and the promo never answers "why should I care?"

* **Avoid:** `skip the intro, just list all six features back to back`
* **Instead:** `hook stating the problem, then 3 feature beats, then the CTA end card`

**Assuming the agent knows your assets.** Without a URL to capture there's no site to read; an unnamed logo or color is invented.

* **Avoid:** `use our brand colors`
* **Instead:** `brand colors #5E6AD2 on off-black; logo at assets/logo.svg`

> [card] [Practice it: Name the scene, say what it becomes](https://hyperframes.heygen.com/lessons/name-the-scene)
>
> Free 20-minute lesson with a short video, a quiz and a brief to try. Swap taste words for things you can see: colors, speeds, moves, seconds.

## Keep the product and its details connected

A full interface shows where the task happens. A close-up makes the important action readable. Ask for both when isolated feature shots lose the sense of a complete product:

```text theme={null}
Show the real workspace, bring the relevant chart and result forward,
then carry the result back into the interface. Build the changing parts
separately, with short explanations where needed. Keep the actual labels
and values; do not invent controls or interactions.
```

For example, a monitoring film can establish the dashboard, draw its signal,
reveal a diagnosis, and return that result to the report view. The product's
real screens or supplied source must support that flow. The surrounding
interface gives context; the close-up carries the labels and numbers the viewer
needs to read.

If a draft feels like slides, ask the agent to change what happens within each
shot: reveal the signal, populate the result, or open the panel before moving
on. Adding camera movement over the same still page does not show the action.
Keep a short explanation of what changed rather than removing all text.

For a color revision, name the background you want and ask the agent to adapt
text and charts across every scene and transition. Check that labels remain
readable and that a later animation does not bring the old background back.

## Review the result

* Every product claim is current.
* The screens shown are realistic and use no private material.
* The interface stays readable while the video plays.
* Close-ups connect to the whole product, and components remain clear while moving between the two views.
* The opening proves the product quickly, and the ending asks for one clear action.

Then [change it](/studio-app/edit-with-the-agent): ask the agent, point at the picture in the Studio app, or edit by hand.


# Remove a video background
Source: https://hyperframes.heygen.com/guides/remove-background

Cut a person or any object out of a clip or picture so titles can pass behind them: in the Studio app with a right-click, or free on your computer with one command.

Cut a person out so titles can pass behind them, lift an object out of a shot, or replace what's behind. The basic
cut-out runs on your computer: no upload, no account, no cost.

<video aria-label="A presenter cut out of a real room, shown against the original and magnified at the hard edges" />

*A presenter cut out of a real room, with the hard edges (hair, a shoulder a plant overlapped) magnified.*

## In the Studio app

Right-click a video or picture in the preview:

* **Cut out object here** lifts out whatever you clicked, a person or a thing. On a video it follows that object
  through the clip. Shift-click adds to the selection; on a picture, **B** brushes the edges. It runs on a Mac:
  pictures on Apple silicon with macOS 14 or later, or Intel with macOS 13.3 or later; video on Apple silicon only.
* **Remove background** keeps the person and drops the rest. It's free and runs on your computer, made for people on plain
  backgrounds. With a HeyGen API key you can choose a cloud cut through HeyGen instead, paid from your API balance.

Or just ask: "put the title behind her", "remove the cup from the table", "put her on a rainy street at night".

## On the command line

```bash theme={null}
npx hyperframes remove-background subject.mp4 -o subject.webm
```

The first run downloads the model; it needs FFmpeg. Pick the output by where it goes: `.webm` for HyperFrames and the
web, `.mov` (ProRes 4444) for Premiere, Resolve or Final Cut, `.png` for a single photo.

For text behind the person, make the cut-out and a background plate with a person-shaped hole in one pass, then
stack: plate, your text or graphic, cut-out on top.

```bash theme={null}
npx hyperframes remove-background subject.mp4 -o subject.webm --background-output plate.webm
```

![The original presenter frame beside its transparent cutout over a green background](https://static.heygen.ai/hyperframes-oss/docs/images/showcase/remove-background-before-after-v1.png)

The same real frame before and after the local model. The softer hair and hand edges are the model’s actual limit on this source.

## When it works, and when it won't

The free model is made for people: a clear subject, steady framing, some contrast with the background. Expect trouble
with a held object (a dark mic or phone can vanish), fine hair over a busy background, and fast motion. For objects,
use **Cut out object here** in the app instead.

## Fixes, quality and speed

| Problem | What to check |
| - | - |
| The background is still opaque | Confirm the output is transparent WebM, MOV, or PNG and preview it over a colored background. |
| Edges flicker | Use a cleaner source, reduce fast movement, or use a stronger external matting tool. |
| Processing is slow | Check `--info`; CPU processing works but is much slower than an available accelerated provider. |
| The subject has a color halo | Use `--quality best`, especially when layering over the original source. |
| The “background plate” has a hole | Expected: it is inverse alpha, not an inpainted clean plate. |
| Part of a held object is missing | The model matches people, not what they hold. Use another matting tool for that shot. |

`--quality best` for a cut-out over its own original footage, `fast` for a smaller file over something unrelated;
`--info` shows whether a fast local processor was found. To move the cut-out, animate a wrapper around the video,
not the video itself. Every flag is in the [CLI reference](/packages/cli#remove-background).

* [Add an AI avatar presenter](/guides/avatar-presenter)
