# Install the Studio app
Source: https://hyperframes.heygen.com/studio-app/index

Download the HyperFrames Studio app for Mac, Windows or Linux, open it for the first time, and sign in with your HeyGen account.

The HyperFrames Studio app for Mac, Windows and Linux is the easiest way to make a video with HyperFrames. You describe the video, an
agent on your computer builds it, and you change it by typing, pointing at the picture, drawing, or commenting.
You do not need to write code. Framey, the small
green guide, points you to the next step along the way.

* **Free.** You sign in with a free HeyGen account.
* **Mac:** Apple Silicon or Intel. **Linux:** 64-bit Intel and AMD, as a .deb or an AppImage.
* **Windows:** 64-bit Intel and AMD, as a zip. Windows on Arm runs the same download through Windows' built-in
  emulation.

![The HyperFrames Studio app's Home screen: the Make something box and the Remix from inspiration feed](https://mintcdn.com/hyperframes/NPYo6ccLFQ7ztD9h/public/images/studio-app/home.jpg?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=NPYo6ccLFQ7ztD9h\&q=85\&s=6c94e122fea75f4e504f69110efb4912)

Home: the Make something box with its Make, Reference and Script tabs, and Remix from inspiration beside it.

## Download and install

> [tab] Mac
>
> **1. Download**
>
> [Download the app for Mac](https://hyperframes.studio/studio/download?os=mac\&src=docs-install). One file works on
> Apple Silicon and Intel Macs.
>
> **2. Install**
>
> Open the downloaded disk image and double-click **Install HyperFrames**. The installer copies the app into
> Applications and shows **Checking it is really from HeyGen**, which can take a minute or two. When it says
> **HyperFrames is in Applications**, choose **Open HyperFrames**.
>
> If your Mac's Applications folder is locked for your account, the installer puts the app in the Applications
> folder inside your home folder instead. If it says **The download looks damaged**, choose **Download again**. If
> it says the check **took too long**, nothing was installed: choose **Try again**.

> [tab] Windows
>
> **1. Download**
>
> [Download the app for Windows](https://hyperframes.studio/studio/download?os=windows\&src=docs-install). You get
> `HyperFrames-win-x64.zip`.
>
> **2. Unzip it and open it**
>
> Right-click the zip and choose **Extract All**. Open the `HyperFrames-win32-x64` folder it makes and
> double-click `HyperFrames.exe`. The app updates itself from there.

> [tab] Linux
>
> **1. Download**
>
> [Download the app for Linux](https://hyperframes.studio/studio/download?os=deb\&src=docs-install).
> You get `HyperFrames-amd64.deb` for 64-bit Intel and AMD computers on Debian, Ubuntu and their
> relatives.
>
> **2. Install it and open it**
>
> In a terminal, in the folder you downloaded it to:
>
> ```bash theme={null}
> sudo apt install ./HyperFrames-amd64*.deb
> ```
>
> Then open **HyperFrames** from your app menu.
>
> Prefer one portable file, or not on a Debian-based system? [Download the AppImage](https://hyperframes.studio/studio/download?os=linux\&src=docs-install)
> instead, then in the folder you downloaded it to:
>
> ```bash theme={null}
> chmod +x HyperFrames-x86_64*.AppImage
> ./HyperFrames-x86_64*.AppImage
> ```
>
> The AppImage is the whole app. Keep it anywhere you like and open it the same way next time.

## First launch

1. A short survey asks what you want to make and which agent you use. Every answer is optional, and **Skip all**
   counts as an answer. What you pick decides where **Build your video** opens. The agent you name starts your first
   chat if it is already set up.
2. Home opens with the **Create your first video** card. See
   [Make your first video](/studio-app/first-video).

A notice also explains what usage data the app records. Choose **Got it** to dismiss it.

## Sign in with HeyGen

On first launch, the app asks you to sign in the first time you click something after the survey.

1. Choose **Continue with HeyGen**. Your browser opens hyperframes.dev.
2. Sign in there within 10 minutes. The browser sends you back to the app, which shows **You're in!** and carries
   on with what you clicked.

If the sign-in runs out of time, choose **Continue with HeyGen** again. If you choose **Not now**, the app asks
again on your next click.
You can sign in or out at any time from **Settings** > **Account**.

## Updates

<video aria-label="Settings, Updates: Check for updates" />

The app updates itself. When a new version is ready, a round button appears in the bottom-right corner; click it and
the app restarts as soon as nothing is running, reopening the project you had open. To check by hand, use
**Settings** > **Updates** > **Check for updates**. If an update stalls, click the button again and choose **Try
again**, or **Download it instead**.

## Where your work is kept

* **Projects**: the hidden `.hyperframes-studio` folder in your home folder, or the folder you imported them from.
  Each one is a normal HyperFrames project, so it also opens in the [browser editor](/studio/index) and the
  [command line](/developers/cli).
* **Exported videos**: your Downloads folder.
* **Settings and sign-in**: `~/Library/Application Support/HyperFrames` on a Mac, `%APPDATA%\HyperFrames` on Windows,
  `~/.config/HyperFrames` on Linux.

## Related topics

* [Connect your agent](/studio-app/connect-your-agent)
* [Make your first video](/studio-app/first-video)
* [Troubleshooting](/help#in-the-studio-app)


# Reference any video to recreate its style
Source: https://hyperframes.heygen.com/studio-app/reference-video

Give the Studio app a video you like, from a link, a file or the inspiration feed. It copies the cuts, captions and effects, and you swap in your own people, words and brand.

Found a video whose editing you love? Give it to the Studio app. Your video gets its cuts, captions and effects, with
your own people, words and brand in it. Showing a video once is faster than describing it, and a video you only half
like is still a better start than a blank page.

<video aria-label="Reference any video: copy its editing style, choose who's on camera, say what it's about" />

*Pick a reference from the feed: it's a person talking to camera, so the app goes to **Copy editing style**. Choose who's
on camera, then say what the video should talk about.*

Reference uses your HeyGen API key: the app watches the video through HeyGen, which uses your API balance. Add the
key in **Settings** > **HeyGen API key**, or when the app asks.

## 1. Pick the video

On Home, open **Reference**. Then:

* **Paste any URL**, then **Use link**. One public video from YouTube (a video or a Short), TikTok, Instagram or X, up to 30 minutes, or a
  published HyperFrames project.
* **Upload your reference**: drop a file from your computer.
* **Pick a reference** from the feed beside it, videos made to be remixed (also on Home as **Remix from inspiration**).

## 2. The app reads it and picks the way

The app watches the reference and decides how to remake it:

* **A person talking to camera** becomes **Copy editing style**: your video gets its cuts, captions and effects, with
  your footage or an AI avatar.
* **Graphics and animation with nobody on camera** becomes a **Video brief**: it recreates the motion with your topic
  and files.

If it can't tell, it asks you to choose between those two, then **Continue**.

## 3. Say what it's about

For **Copy editing style**, the app asks **Who's on camera?**

* **Upload your own takes.** Add **Editing instructions** if you want, for example "Cut the pauses, keep it under 30
  seconds".
* **An AI avatar:** your photo or a HeyGen presenter. Say what the avatar should say; a sentence or two is enough.

For a **Video brief**, write **What will your video talk about** (a sentence or two), and add your own pictures or
clips with **Upload assets**.

## 4. Swap what should be yours

**What to swap** lists the parts the app found in the reference, each with where it appears, for example "Your
opening question 0:00-0:02" or "Your website URL 0:02-0:05". Choose how to fill each:

| Choice | What happens |
| - | - |
| **Framey writes it** / **Framey decides** | Framey fills it to fit your topic |
| **Type yours** | Write the exact words |
| **Upload** | Use your own file |
| **Generate** | Make a picture or clip. Its price shows under the row once you pick it |

Choose a brand kit for the video, or **No brand kit**. Your workspace default stays as you set it. Then **Continue**;
Framey may ask a question or two about anything the video leaves open.

## 5. Compare with the original

While Framey builds, **Show original** at the top of the preview plays the reference over the picture. When the
build is done, the same button sets the two side by side, on one clock, so you can see what matches and what doesn't.
Then [edit the result](/studio-app/edit-with-the-agent) like any other video.

## Use other people's videos fairly

The app copies the editing style, not the footage: your video is built from your own takes, avatar, words and
media. Don't reuse the original's footage, music or logos unless you have the rights to them.

## Related topics

* [What to make](/workflows)
* [Edit a video with the agent](/studio-app/edit-with-the-agent)
* [Add a brand kit](/studio-app/brand-kits)


# Share your video for review
Source: https://hyperframes.heygen.com/studio-app/share

Get feedback on a video from the HyperFrames Studio app: one click makes a review link people can watch and comment on. Choose who can open it, send new versions on the same link, or turn it off.

**Share** in the project's top bar turns your latest export into a review page and copies its link. Send it to
anyone who should watch or comment. When you change the video, the new version goes on the same link.

<video aria-label="Share: pick who can open the link, then turn it off" />

*Share, then **Who has access**: Only you, people you invite, your workspace, or anyone with the link. Turn off link
ends it for everyone.*

## Share a link

<video aria-label="Share in the top bar" />

Choose **Share**. The app uploads your last MP4 export, makes the review page and copies its link. If there's no
MP4 yet, it opens the Export panel first and shares as soon as the export finishes. See
[export a video](/studio-app/export).

Then HeyGen checks the video before reviewers can see it. The panel shows **Checking…**, which can take a few minutes.

You need to be signed in to HeyGen. The link is made in the workspace you're signed in to, named under **Shares to**;
choose **Change** to move it to another one.

## Choose who can open it

By default, **anyone in your workspace with the link can comment**. To change it, choose the row under **Who has
access**:

| Choice | Who can open it |
| - | - |
| **Only you** | Nobody else |
| **Only people you invite** | They sign in with the invited email |
| **Anyone in** your workspace | People signed in to that workspace, not people from outside |
| **Anyone with the link** | No sign-in. Guests type a name to comment |

Next to it, choose **can comment** or **can only watch**. Pick **Only you** before you share something that isn't ready
for others.

## Send a new version

When the project has changed since the version on the review page, the panel says so. Export an MP4, then choose
**Add this version**. It's the same link: everyone who has it sees the new version.
**Open review page** opens it in your browser. For a link anyone can open, the button is **View as reviewer** and
shows the page signed out, as your guests see it.

## Turn off the link

Choose **Turn off link**, then confirm. Everyone loses access at once, and the comments are kept. **Turn on with a new
link** shares it again under a new link.

## Related topics

* [Export a video](/studio-app/export)
* [Edit a video with the agent](/studio-app/edit-with-the-agent)


# Make clips with HeyGen Video 1
Source: https://hyperframes.heygen.com/studio-app/video-clips

Generate an AI video clip up to a minute long with HeyGen Video 1 in the HyperFrames Studio app, and put it straight into your project.

**HeyGen Video 1** generates one unbroken shot from a description, up to a minute long. The clip lands in your
project's files, and the agent places it on the timeline.

## Ask the agent for a clip

<video aria-label="Tools (#), then HeyGen Video 1" />

**1. Open Tools**

In the chat, type **#** to open **HyperFrames tools**, then pick **HeyGen Video 1**.

**2. Set the length**

Choose the length pill to open **Length in seconds**. A clip can be 5 to 60 seconds; it starts at 15.

**3. Describe the shot**

Say what happens, how the camera moves and how it should look, then send. The agent makes the clip and puts it on
the timeline.

You can steer the clip in the same message:

* **Start from a picture**: give an image and it becomes the clip's exact first frame.
* **Match a look**: give up to 9 reference images.
* **Copy a movement**: give one reference video of 5 seconds or less (trim a longer one first; the app refuses it), plus a picture of the person who should do the move. The clip is then one take of up to 15 seconds, with no start picture.
* **Shape**: 16:9, 9:16 or 1:1, at 480p or 768p (768p is the default).

## Or use Generate media

**Generate media** makes a clip without a chat message. Find it on an empty timeline, or in the words bar. Choose **Video**, pick the **Video 1** model,
set **Quality**, and add a **Start from** picture if you want one. This form makes clips of 5 to 15 seconds, in 16:9 or
9:16. The same form also offers **H3 Max** and **Seedance**.

## Change a clip you already have

Select a video in the preview and choose **Generate media** in the bar above it. Describe the change ("make it snow",
"turn it into a night scene") and choose **Make**. The bar shows what it will cost at most and what's left on your key
before you start.

<video aria-label="Select a clip, Generate media, describe the change, Make" />

*"Make it snow": HeyGen Video 1 whitened the roof and gave her a new movement, and the new clip lands in Media.
The wait is sped up.*

Keep the clip small: a 5-second 1080p file of 7.8 MB came back with **The references are too large to send**, while
the same shot at 720p went through.

## What it costs

In the chat, the agent makes the clip as soon as you ask, without a separate price check; the **Generate media**
form shows the price before you start. It is paid from your HyperFrames plan when
the plan covers it, otherwise from the HeyGen API credits on the key in **Settings**.

If a clip stops with **Out of API credits**, add credits in HeyGen and try again. If it asks you to set up your key,
add your HeyGen API key in **Settings**, or choose a plan.

## Related topics

* [Add an AI avatar presenter to a video](/guides/avatar-presenter)
* [Use images and video](/guides/video-components)
* [Edit a video with the agent](/studio-app/edit-with-the-agent)


# Find your way around a project
Source: https://hyperframes.heygen.com/studio-app/workspace

Every part of a Studio app project: the chat and its @, # and / menus, the Script panel that edits video like a document, Media, Captions, Inspirations and Layers.

A project has three columns: the chat with your agent on the left, the preview in the middle, and panels on the
right. The timeline opens under the preview with **Show timeline**.

## The chat box: @, # and /

Three keys open menus right where you type.

<video aria-label="Typing @ opens the menu of things to add" />

**`@` adds something to your message.** The menu groups everything the agent can use: **Media** you added,
**Scenes & brand kit**, **Inspirations** (moments from real videos), **Captions** styles, **Voices**, other
**Projects**, **Tools**, or **Add files from your Mac** (**your PC** on Windows). Press **Tab** to jump between groups. Whatever you pick shows as a chip
above your words, so the agent knows exactly which file or style you mean.

<video aria-label="Typing # opens HyperFrames tools" />

**`#` picks a tool** for this request: **Storyboard**, **Brand kit**, **HeyGen Voice 1**, **Remove background**,
**HeyGen Video 1**, **Reference video** or **Create assets** (some accounts also see **Podcast edit** and **Computer
use**). Use it when
you want a specific job done the specific way ("#Remove background on the presenter, then put the title behind her").
The HeyGen ones bill your HeyGen plan when it covers them, otherwise the HeyGen API key in **Settings**.

<video aria-label="Typing / opens commands and skills" />

**`/` runs a command or turns on a skill.** **/clear** starts a fresh chat (earlier messages stay above) and
in Claude Code, **/compact** shortens a long one. Below them are ready-made video formats (founder take, AI breakdown reel, cards
behind you, behind-head captions and more) and any skills you have installed: picking one turns it on for the project.

<video aria-label="The Skills menu in the chat header" />

The chat header shows which agent, model and effort the next request uses (click to change), and **Skills** lists
what the agent can use: HyperFrames' own (always on), **Talking-head formats** and **Video workflows** that work only
when picked, and **Your skills** from Claude Code or Codex.

## Script: edit the video like a document

Open **Script** at the top of the right panel (on some accounts it opens from a clip's menu instead). Every word
spoken in your video appears as text. The audio is sent to HeyGen to transcribe it, so this needs your HeyGen sign-in
on a plan that includes it, or a HeyGen API key in **Settings**.

Select words (click the first, Shift-click the last), then choose **Cut** or press <kbd>⌫</kbd>. The words stay in
the script, struck through, and the cut waits under **Pending video edits** above the chat box with anything else you
staged. Choose **Send 1 edit** (the count grows as you stage more) and the agent applies them all; the video gets shorter once it's done. To drop a
cut before sending, delete its row in **Pending video edits**. To bring back words already cut, select them, choose
**Restore**, and send that too.

<video aria-label="Cut a sentence in the script, then send it to the agent" />

With words selected, the bar offers:

* **Comment**: a note on those words for the agent.
* **Cut** (or **Restore** on cut words).
* **Fix words**: correct what the transcript heard. The audio stays the same.
* **Add**: a **Zoom in**, a **B-roll shot** or a **Title card** on those words.
* **Make clip** (podcast projects): cut the words into a vertical clip of their own.
* **Ask**: ask your agent about those words.

When the agent spots filler or repeated takes, the top of the script shows how many cuts it suggests and how much
shorter they'd make the video, with **Keep all** and **Cut all**. Click a suggested cut to see why, and keep or cut
just that one.

## Media, Captions, Inspirations, Layers

The row of icons at the top of the right panel, **All files**, **Captions**, **Inspirations**, **Layers** (and
**Reviews** where review is on), switches what the panel shows:

<video aria-label="The Captions panel" />

**Captions:** 91 caption styles. Click one to use it in the chat, then say where it goes.

<video aria-label="The Inspirations panel" />

**Inspirations:** moments from real videos (motion graphics, A-roll cuts, mobile ads, shaders), with ideas for whatever you selected.

<video aria-label="The Layers panel" />

**Layers:** every element in the video, top to bottom; pick one to select it in the preview.

**Media** lists the project's files by folder. Add one to the chat to talk about it ("use this as the background"),
and use the plus button to bring in files from your computer.

## Framey

Framey, the small green character by the preview, shows what your agent is doing and tells you when a video is ready
or needs you. Change how it looks in **Settings** > **Framey**.

## The preview tools

Under the preview: **Select** to click any element (right-click it for **Ask Framey**, layer order, **Cut out object
here** on footage, on a Mac with Apple silicon), **Draw** to circle what should change, and **Comment** to leave a note at a moment. Changes stack
up and go to the agent together; see [edit a video with the agent](/studio-app/edit-with-the-agent).

## Related topics

* [Edit a video with the agent](/studio-app/edit-with-the-agent)
* [Remove a background](/guides/remove-background)
* [Use your brand kit](/studio-app/brand-kits)


# Captions, assets and variables
Source: https://hyperframes.heygen.com/studio/assets-and-blocks

In the browser editor: import and reuse media, add Catalog visuals, restyle caption words, and turn values into variables for templates.

Use **Assets** for media files. Use **Catalog** for reusable visual scenes and components.

<video />

Import project media, then add a compatible Catalog scene at the playhead.

## Import an asset

1. Open **Assets**.
2. Choose **Import media**, or drop files into the panel.
3. Preview it before adding it to the project.
4. Drag it to the timeline or use it from the relevant inspector control.

Keep clear filenames. `product-dashboard-dark.png` is easier to reuse than `Screenshot 42.png`.

## Reuse project assets

**This project** contains the files available to the open project. **All projects** is a read-only
index of the global `~/.media` cache, where resolved media can be found again across projects. It is
not a file manager, so files cannot be deleted or replaced from that view.

If a large video is still preparing a preview or proxy, wait for that process before judging playback performance.

## Add a Catalog item

Open **Catalog**, search or pick a category (**Captions**, **Code Animations**, **VFX**, **Transitions**, **Effects**)
and preview what you need. Choose **Add** where it's offered to place it at the playhead, or **Ask agent** to copy a
ready request for your agent, which adapts the item to your composition. Then swap the sample content for yours and
match the project's timing and look.

Browse the full [Catalog](/catalog) when you want to compare categories and individual examples.

> [!TIP]
>
> Reusable does not mean finished. Remove sample content and decorative motion that does not support
> your story.

## Edit captions

When a composition has captions, the editor switches to caption editing: click a word on the frame, or find it in the
caption track under the preview.

![HyperFrames browser editor with one caption word selected, word blocks in the caption rail, and position and transform controls](https://static.heygen.ai/hyperframes-oss/docs/images/studio-captions-panel-v1.jpg)

A selected word connects the canvas, caption rail, and the controls that the browser editor currently saves.

### What you can change here

Select a word (Shift-click for more), then drag, resize or rotate it on the frame. Arrow keys nudge it by 1 pixel,
Shift + arrow by 10. Color, opacity, font size, weight and family are in the panel. These edits are saved for you, in
`caption-overrides.json`, a moment after you make them.

### What to ask the agent for

Wording, timing, how words are grouped into lines and the caption style itself live in the caption source, not in
the editor. Ask your agent ("break the captions into two-word groups", "fix the spelling of HeyGen") or change the
source.

Then watch once with sound and once muted: names and numbers right, nothing covering a face or a button, and the last
caption clearing cleanly. For reusable styles, browse [caption components](/catalog/components/caption-highlight).

## Use variables

Variables let one project produce many versions without rebuilding its layout or animation.

![HyperFrames browser editor showing a composition beside the Variables panel with Title, Subtitle, and Background inputs](https://static.heygen.ai/hyperframes-oss/docs/images/studio-variables-panel-v1.jpg)

The current Variables panel previews values beside the real composition.

### Create one reusable input

The quickest path starts from the canvas:

1. Select the element.
2. Open **Variables** in the right panel.
3. Bind the text, media source, text color, background, or font property.
4. Create a new variable or choose a compatible existing one.

Before binding to an existing variable, the browser editor shows its saved default, using the font name or image URL for object values.

For a value that is not tied to the selected element, click **Add variable**. The browser editor supports string, number, color, boolean, enum, font, and image variables. Number variables can include minimum, maximum, and step values; enums can define their allowed options.

Name the input by meaning—`customerName`, `headline`, or `brandColor`—rather than by its position in the design.

### Preview without changing the template

Change a value in the Variables panel to preview that version immediately. The preview is an override: it does not replace the saved default.

The panel tells you whether you are previewing defaults or custom values. Use **Reset** to clear all preview overrides. When a scalar preview should become the new default, use **Set default**.

Use **Edit** to change a variable's label, description, or saved default. For font and image objects, **Default** edits the font name or image URL. Saving keeps the font source, image alt text and fit, and any other stored metadata, including when you change only the label or description.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Variables from other compositions are listed separately. You can edit their declarations, but
> their values are not live-previewed in the active composition.

### Hand the project off

At the bottom of the panel, **Use this template** can copy either:

* the effective values as JSON;
* a ready-to-run `npx hyperframes render ... --variables ...` command.

This keeps the values you just reviewed attached to the render request instead of asking the next person to reconstruct them.

### Test the fallback

A useful template survives realistic variation. Before handing it off, test:

* long and short names or headlines;
* image aspect ratios;
* color contrast;
* number formatting;
* missing optional values.

For the schema, HTML bindings, and batch-render examples, read [Variables](/concepts/variables).

# Mix audio
Source: https://hyperframes.heygen.com/studio/audio-effects

In the browser editor: effects and presets on a track, music that sits under narration, groups, muting, and automation over time.

The browser editor carries a full mixer. Every audio track has an effect rack: filters that
decide which frequencies it may occupy, dynamics that decide how its level
behaves, character effects that change the shape of the waveform, and space
effects that put it somewhere.

Everything you do here is written into the composition's HTML. There is no
separate session file, so a mix survives being handed to someone else, committed,
or rendered on another machine.

## Effects and presets

### Open a track's effect rack

Select an audio clip on the timeline. The right panel shows an **Audio FX**
section for it, listing the chain from top to bottom in signal order and ending
in **Out to mix**. An empty track reads "No effects on this track."

Do not confuse it with the **Effects** section on the same panel — that one is
visual effects for pictures, and has nothing to do with sound.

You can also reach it without the panel: the **FX** button on an audio track's
timeline header opens a shelf of presets, with **Open rack ›** at the bottom. The
button shows a count when the track already has effects.

### Fix a voice with one preset

Presets are the fastest honest answer to "this voice sounds wrong". Each one is
an ordinary chain you could have built by hand — open it and the individual
effects are all showing.

Start from the symptom rather than the effect list:

| It sounds like | Reach for |
| - | - |
| Hum or thump underneath | `rumble-cut`, or a high-pass at 80 Hz |
| Boomy, chesty, too close to the mic | **Tame Boominess** |
| Muffled, like it is behind cardboard | **Reduce Mud** |
| Words hard to make out | **Add Clarity**, or [carve the music](/studio/audio-effects#make-music-sit-under-narration) |
| Harsh and tiring over a whole listen | **Soften Harshness** |
| Some words much louder than others | **Evenness** on a compressor, or **Even Out Levels** |
| Room tone audible between sentences | `room-gate` |
| Voice and music fighting each other | [A carve on the music](/studio/audio-effects#make-music-sit-under-narration) — not an EQ on either |
| Dry, recorded nowhere | `room-tight` or `room-natural` |
| Just "amateur" | `voice-clean` |

`voice-clean` is the default answer to "fix this voiceover": it removes rumble,
reduces mud, evens the level, adds clarity, and ends in a peak ceiling.
`voice-broadcast` is the same idea denser and more forward; `voice-warm` adds
body instead of cutting it.

Applying a preset **appends** to the chain, so cleaning a voice and then adding
character is a real thing to do. Re-applying the same preset replaces its own
nodes where they already sit.

Every named job also ships inside a preset at identical settings, so check what a
preset already contains before adding a job on top of it — `voice-clean` plus a
Reduce Mud job is −6 dB at 250 Hz where −3 was meant. Expanding the preset in the
rack shows its nodes by name, which is the fastest way to see it.

Beyond the corrective families there are **Character** presets — `telephone`,
`radio-am`, `megaphone`, `lofi-tape`, `pa-system`, `intercom`, `doofus-worble`,
`chipmunk`, `giant`, `monster` — and **Space** presets — `room-tight`, `room-natural`, `hall`, `slap-echo`,
`dub-throw`. Character presets are costumes rather than corrections, and they are
tuned to be distinguishable from one another, so do not stack two. `chipmunk`,
`giant`, and `monster` shift pitch, so they change who is speaking rather than
what they are speaking through.

### Add a single effect

Use **+ effect** in the rack. The menu groups effects the way you would reach for
them, in four families:

| Family | Decides |
| - | - |
| **Filters** | Which frequencies the track may occupy |
| **Dynamics** | How its level behaves over time |
| **Non-linear** | The shape of the waveform — character and grit |
| **Time** | Where it sits and how it moves: delay, reverb, chorus, phaser, and pitch shift |

The menu offers the [named jobs](#fix-a-voice-with-one-preset) in place of a bare
`peaking` filter, because picking `peaking` is picking a machine and leaving the
real decision — which frequency range — for afterwards.

Order matters, because each effect processes what the one before produced. Work in
this order and each step hears a cleaner signal than it otherwise would:

1. **Subtract before you add.** Cut rumble and mud first. A voice that sounds dull
   often has too much low-mid rather than too little top.
2. **Level after you filter.** A compressor reacts to whatever is loudest, and a
   rumble it can no longer see is a rumble it stops chasing.
3. **Relationships after level.** Carve the music once the voice itself is
   settled.
4. **Character, then ceiling.** Saturation and space go late; a limiter goes last,
   where it can actually act as a ceiling. Anything after it is not bounded by it.

Rename any node so the rack says what it is doing. Two `peaking` rows otherwise
look identical and you cannot tell the mud cut from the clarity lift.

Bypass a node instead of deleting it while you are deciding — it stays in the
chain, out of the signal path, so you can compare without losing the settings.

### Use the one-knob controls

Five effects have no single parameter that could honestly be their face — a
compressor's threshold means nothing without its ratio. Those show one derived
knob instead:

| Effect | Knob | 0 → 1 |
| - | - | - |
| Compressor | **Evenness** | Barely touched → very even, quite squashed |
| Gate | **Tightness** | Only true silence → cuts quiet words too |
| Saturation | **Warmth** | Just a sheen → openly distorted |
| Reverb | **Space** | A small tight room → a big open hall |
| Bitcrush | **Crush** | Slightly gritty → destroyed |

Evenness, Warmth, and Space are level-matched: the make-up gain, output trim, and
dry leg move with the drive, so turning the knob up does not also turn the track
up. Tightness and Crush are not, because neither has a trim to move.

Editing a parameter underneath one of these knobs is allowed and simply moves the
knob — the chain stores the mechanism, not the knob position.

### Even out a drifting take

**Even Out Levels** measures the track's own speaking passages and writes a gain
envelope. Its target is that track's own 80th percentile rather than an absolute
level, so an already-even track is left alone. Use it when passages drift over a
whole take; use a compressor's **Evenness** when the problem is word-to-word
dynamics. **Remove levelling** takes it back off.

### What should happen

* Preview is what the render will sound like: both build the same graph from the
  same attributes.
* A chain the browser editor cannot read plays **dry** in preview so the composition stays
  workable — but it **fails the render** rather than shipping a track that sounds
  plausible and is wrong. If preview sounds unprocessed, suspect the chain.
* Reverb and delay make a track **longer** than its source. A bed with reverb no
  longer ends exactly at its clip length; that is expected.

### Common problems

**Nothing sounds different.** Check the node is not bypassed, then check you are
looking at **Audio FX** rather than the visual **Effects** section.

**The voice got louder as well as cleaner.** A preset ending in a peak ceiling
raises perceived loudness. Trim the track's own level rather than removing the
ceiling.

**A cut landed twice.** A preset already contained the job you added on top.
Expand the preset and read its nodes by name.

**It sounds worse after adding top end.** A muddy voice needs the low-mid cut
first; lifting the top of a muddy voice makes it muddy *and* harsh.

**There is hiss under the words.** Nothing here removes it. A gate closes the gaps
between phrases and leaves the noise beneath speech untouched — a source with
audible hiss needs a better source.

## Make music sit under narration

Music under narration is the most common audio problem in a video, and the
obvious fix is the wrong one.

Turning the whole music track down works, and it costs the music all of its
presence for as long as anyone is talking — the bed goes limp through the entire
voiceover. But a voice does not need the whole spectrum. It needs the few bands it
actually occupies. A **carve** takes only those out of the music, so the bed keeps
its low end and its top: still music, while the voice stays intelligible.

### When to use it

Whenever a music bed plays under speech. It is not a polish step to reach if
there is time — place both tracks, carve, and listen.

Skip it only when there is no narration for the music to sit under: a music video,
a title card, a montage cut to the track.

### Carve a bed

The carve is a module at the top of the **music** track's rack, not a separate
tool. Select the music clip, open its **Audio FX** section, and the module asks
you to pick the voices this bed should make room for.

A bed with exactly one candidate voice above it is **already carved**, at the
default strength, because that is what a bed under narration wants. Several
candidates leaves the picker waiting rather than guessing which one is the voice.

> [!WARNING]
>
> The carve belongs on the **music**, never on the voice. It names the tracks it
> makes room for, the same way a sidechain compressor does — you select the track
> that gets quieter and pick what makes it quieter. A voice carved against itself
> is a bug, not a subtle mix choice.

### Set the strength

One control does the whole job. It derives how deep to cut, how many bands, how
wide they are, how far the level may drop, and how far under the voice to aim —
because those move together in any real mix.

| Strength | What you get |
| - | - |
| Default (0.25) | A 6 dB dip in three bands — audible without sounding like a hole |
| Around 0.5 | The dip reaches 10 dB, where a carve starts being heard as an effect |
| Higher | Deliberate territory for a loud bed under a quiet voice |
| 0 | Spectral only — one band, no level matching at all |

**Switch the carve off** keeps the settings and stops the carve, which is
different from clearing it: a bed with one candidate voice would otherwise be
carved again by default the moment it was re-evaluated.

### What it writes

Ordinary effects. Open the rack after carving and you will find a few `peaking`
filters and a `gain` stage — nothing hidden, nothing proprietary.

Two things follow from that:

* **The envelopes are editable.** The carve always follows the speech, so every
  value becomes an automation lane you can adjust by hand afterwards. Silence
  leaves the music alone; a loud passage pushes the carve to full depth. There is
  no fixed-depth mode, because a fixed dip thins the bed through every pause.
* **Re-carving is safe.** The nodes a carve writes are tagged as its own, so
  running it again at a new strength replaces exactly those and leaves every
  effect and lane you built by hand where it was.

Inside a carved bed the signal runs through the dips first, then the level match,
then anything you added yourself — which is why a limiter you place stays the last
ceiling.

### Point it at a group, not at clips

If narration arrives as several clips, [group them](/studio/audio-effects#group-tracks) and
carve against the group.

A carve pointed at individual clips has to list every one of them, and it stays
right only until the next edit: add a fourth narration clip and it plays outside
the carve's awareness, so the music silently fails to duck under it. A carve
pointed at a group resolves membership every time the analysis runs, so a clip
added later is covered without touching the carve.

The browser editor does this for you when you pick a second ungrouped voice — it creates a
group behind them and points the carve at that instead.

### What should happen

* The voice is legible without the bed sounding hollowed out.
* The music comes **back up between phrases** rather than staying flat.
* The bed keeps its bass and its top end. A carve that removed those would just
  be a filter.

### Common problems

**The music sounds notched or hollow.** Strength is too high. Come back toward
the default. This is the one failure mode with an obvious sound.

**The voice is still buried.** A carve cannot fix a bed that is simply louder than
the voice — spectral room does not solve a level problem. Compare the two tracks'
actual loudness first. Machine-generated speech commonly arrives far below a
mastered music track, and that gap is arithmetic rather than taste.

**The bed starts out already ducked.** A lane holds its first value backwards to
the start of its clip. A bed that begins before the voice needs an explicit "no
cut" point at its start.

**The music pumps.** The level envelope releases slowly on purpose, because music
that snaps back the instant a word ends sounds like a machine doing it. If it
still pumps, the gaps between phrases are shorter than the release — lower the
strength rather than fighting the envelope.

**Nothing was carved.** The picker leaves itself alone when several tracks could
be the voice. Name the voice explicitly.

## Group tracks

Five narration clips usually want one set of effects and one fader —
not five copies that drift apart as you edit. A group gives them that: its members
sum through a single bus, and the bus carries the group's own volume, effects, and
automation.

### When to use a group

* **Narration in several clips.** One rack for the whole voice, and one thing for
  a [carve](/studio/audio-effects#make-music-sit-under-narration) to point at.
* **More than a couple of sound effects.** One place to turn all of them down is
  worth more than precise individual levels you will never revisit.
* **Anything you want to turn up or down as a unit** — an ambience layer, a music stem.

A single clip does not need a group. Its own rack is already one place.

### Create a group

On an audio track holding more than one ungrouped clip, the **FX** button offers
to group them first: it reads "Group these clips to add effects to all of them".
Choose **Group**.

The browser editor creates a group behind those clips and points anything that needed it — a
carve, for instance — at the group rather than at the individual clip ids.

### Read a group row

A group gets its own timeline row, carrying:

| Control | Does |
| - | - |
| Caret | Shows or hides the member rows beneath it |
| `▤` and name | The group glyph and its label |
| Count | How many members it holds |
| **FX** | Opens the group's own rack, applying to the summed bus |
| `∿` | Shows or hides [the group's own automation lanes](/studio/audio-effects#automate-over-time) |

The caret and the `∿` toggle are independent: showing a group's members does not
open their automation lanes, and opening the group's lanes does not expand its
members.

A group-level effect hears the **sum** of its members, not each one separately.
That is the point of a bus — one compressor across a whole voiceover behaves
differently from five compressors on five clips, and usually better.

### Mute a track or a clip

On an audio track, the speaker button where a visual track has its eye mutes the
track: **Mute track** and **Unmute track**. For a selected clip, the same toggle sits
at the top of its properties, and the media section has a **Muted** switch.

A group row has no mute of its own; to silence a whole group, mute its members'
tracks. Muted audio is left out of the render, so unmute anything you want in the
export.

### Membership lives on the member

Worth knowing because it explains most surprises: each clip records which group it
belongs to, rather than the group listing its members. Delete a clip and it simply
disappears from the group; nothing dangles.

Groups are **audio only** and do not nest. A group marker on a video clip is
ignored.

### What should happen

* The group row appears with the members collapsed beneath it, and the
  grouping offer disappears from that track's **FX** button.
* Effects added to the group apply to everything under it at once.
* Muting the group silences all members, in preview and in the render.

### Common problems

**The group's effects do nothing.** Check that the members actually carry the
group, rather than that the group appears to list them.

**Nothing happened when I grouped clips.** Grouping resolves the clips it was
given against the timeline's current rows. If the track is collapsed, or its clips
live inside a nested composition, expand it and try again.

**Clips inside a nested composition are not offered grouping.** They arrive as
separate rows rather than as one track holding several clips, so the grouping
offer does not appear. Group them in the composition that owns them.

**A track was missing from the export.** Check whether it is muted: muted audio is
left out of the render.

## Automate over time

A static setting cannot say "quieter while the interview is on screen" or "fade
out over the last three seconds". An automation lane can: it is a set of points on
one parameter, and the value moves between them.

Lanes work on a track's own **volume** and on any supported effect parameter, and
a [group](/studio/audio-effects#group-tracks) has lanes of its own that apply to its whole bus.

### Show a track's lanes

Use the `∿` toggle on the track or group row. It shows a count when lanes already
exist, and it is independent of the row's expand caret — showing a group's members
does not open its lanes.

To start automating an effect parameter, automate it from the parameter's own
control in the rack. A parameter with a lane shows as **Automated**, and its
static control is disabled: the lane owns the value from then on.

### Draw and edit an envelope

Work directly on the lane:

* **Add a point** on the lane at the time you want it.
* **Drag a point** to move it in time or value.
* **Type an exact value** rather than dragging, when the number matters. A volume
  lane can go above unity — the ceiling is +12 dB, not 1.
* **Bend a segment** by dragging its curve, so the value holds and then moves late
  rather than travelling evenly.
* **Select a time range** to work on several points at once.

With a range selected, right-click it for the shape and cleanup menu:

| Item | Does |
| - | - |
| **Ramp up** / **Ramp down** | Replaces the selection with a single move in one direction |
| **Swell** | Rises and returns |
| **Dip** | Falls and returns — the shape most ducking wants |
| **Simplify** | Removes redundant points while keeping the shape. Needs at least three points in the selection |

A selection can also be **copied and pasted** onto another lane, and **retimed** by
stretching its edges — useful when narration moves and its ducking should move
with it.

### Two things that surprise people

**A track lane's times are relative to its clip.** A bed starting at 8 s has its
first point at composition time 8. Move the clip and its envelope moves with it.

**A group lane's times are composition time.** A group has no start of its own,
so its lanes are measured from the beginning of the video. If you are automating
a group bus, read the times as absolute.

**A lane holds its first value backwards** to the start of the clip, and its last
value forward to the end. So a bed that begins before the voice needs an explicit
"no cut" point at the start, or it begins already ducked. This is the single most
common automation mistake.

### Not every knob can move

A parameter can only be automated if the audio engine can schedule it directly.
Three kinds cannot:

| These | Cannot be automated because |
| - | - |
| Compressor, limiter, gate, bitcrush, pitch shift | They are configured whole rather than knob-by-knob — **no parameter on any of them can move** |
| Saturation's type, threshold, and oversample | They rebuild the distortion curve; only its output stage can move |
| Reverb's size and damping | They regenerate the room; its wet and dry levels can move |

**A lane on one of those is silently inert** — it stores fine and never does
anything. Pitch shift is the one that catches people out, because a rising pitch
sounds like something a lane should do: it cannot, and the lane will not report
it. To make a compressor's behaviour change over time, automate a `gain` stage
*before* it instead: that changes how hard the compressor is driven, which
is most of what automating its threshold would have done.

To fade a whole preset in or out, automate the preset itself rather than its
parts — its nodes share no single parameter, so the preset as a unit is the only
handle that works.

The [effect registry](/reference/audio-effects#effect-registry) marks every
parameter that can move.

### What should happen

* The value moves between your points, in preview and in the render identically.
* A parameter with a lane reads **Automated** and its static control is disabled.
* A [carve](/studio/audio-effects#make-music-sit-under-narration) writes lanes of its own, and they are
  ordinary lanes: you can edit them afterwards like any others.

### Common problems

**The lane does nothing.** Either the parameter is one of those above, or the
effect it pointed at is gone. A lane whose effect was deleted is dropped silently
rather than reported.

**A newly added effect arrives already "Automated".** A lane left behind by a
deleted effect can be inherited by the next effect that takes the same internal
id. Remove the stale lane.

**The volume lane is ignored.** A `volume` lane and a timeline tween on the same
track's volume conflict; the lane wins. Pick one.

**The envelope is right but the level is wrong.** A tween's values are absolute
and replace a track's own gain rather than scaling it. Check whether the track
also carries a static level.

**The bed ducks before anyone speaks.** The first point is holding backwards. Add
a point at the clip's start.

## Related topics

* [Audio effects implementation](/reference/audio-effects)


# Edit on the canvas
Source: https://hyperframes.heygen.com/studio/canvas

In the browser editor: select and change what you see, animate it with keyframes, and edit the code or hand it to your agent.

For anything you can point at in the current frame.

![HyperFrames browser editor with a headline selected on the canvas and its Design controls open](https://static.heygen.ai/hyperframes-oss/docs/images/studio/canvas-v1.jpg)

A selected headline exposes canvas handles and the Design controls that apply to it.

## Select it

Pause where the element is fully visible and click it. If the wrong thing gets selected (or it's hidden, off-frame or
inside a group), pick it in the **Layers** tab instead. The selection is the same in the preview, the panels and the
timeline.

## Change it

On the preview: drag inside the selection to move it, drag a handle to resize, use the rotation control, crop an image
or video without moving its box, nudge with the arrow keys. Guides show when it snaps.

For exact values, use **Design**. Its sections depend on what you selected:

| Need | Look in Design |
| - | - |
| Change wording or typography | Text |
| Set position, size, spacing, or alignment | Layout |
| Change fill, border, radius, shadow, opacity, or effects | Style |
| Replace or fit an image, video, or audio source | Media |
| Adjust perspective or 3D transforms | Layout (3D Transform) |
| Correct an image or video's appearance | Grade |
| Change timing or animation | Motion |
| Apply a look or media effect | Effects |

Make one kind of change at a time, play it, then decide on the next.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Auto-record manual edits as keyframes** is on by default, so moving something at one frame can quietly become an
> animation. Turn it off in the timeline toolbar for a fix that should hold for the whole clip.

## Layers, groups and nested scenes

Drag in **Layers** to change what sits in front. Timeline tracks are about time, not stacking. Group things that move
together with **⌘G** (ungroup **⌘⇧G**). Open a nested scene to change the scene itself; stay in the parent to change
only where or when it appears.

## Replace media

Select the image, video or audio and swap the file from **Media** in Design or from **Assets**. Then check the crop,
the length, and the cut in and out: a new file can have another shape or duration.

## Check it playing

Play from before the edit to after it: still readable at the final size, not covering anything important, entrances
and exits still working, text readable over every background it crosses. ⌘Z undoes.

## When it isn't editable here

Some generated or nested elements don't expose every property. Try selecting the exact parent or child in Layers, or
open the nested scene. Otherwise choose **Ask agent about this element** in Design (it copies the element and your
request for your agent), or ask for the bigger change directly:

```text theme={null}
Keep this scene's content, but rebuild its layout so the product stays readable at phone size.
```

## Animate with keyframes

A keyframe is a value at a moment; the motion is what happens between two of them. Keyframes show as diamonds on
the timeline.

<video />

Select an element, place the playhead, and add a keyframe.

### Read the motion first

Select the element, expand its animation lanes on the timeline, and play from before the move to after it. Name the
real problem first: it starts late, takes too long, takes the wrong route, or speeds up the wrong way. Each needs a
different fix.

### Add, move or delete keyframes

Put the playhead on the moment, choose **Add keyframe at playhead** (or press **K** with the element selected), and
change the property. Drag a diamond to retime it (closer together is faster), change its value, or press **Delete**.

With **Auto-record manual edits as keyframes** on (the default), any change you make at the playhead becomes a
keyframe. That's the quick way to pose two moments: set the first, move the playhead, set the second, play. Turn it
off for a fix that should hold the whole clip.

### Easing and paths

* **Easing** is how it speeds up and slows down between keyframes. Start from a preset; use the speed curve when the
  start or the stop still feels wrong; use a hold for a jump with no in-between. Judge it playing, not from the curve.
* **Paths:** position keyframes draw a route on the preview. Drag a point to change it, bend a segment to curve it,
  hold **Option** while dragging the element to move the whole path. Turn on auto-rotate only when the element
  should face where it's going.

### Record a gesture

When a move is easier to perform than describe: select the element, press **R** (**Record a gesture**), move the
pointer, press **R** again. Drag records position, scroll records depth; the shortcuts panel lists the keys for
rotation, opacity and scale. Treat it as a first take: simplify the path and retime it.

### Motion the agent wrote

Some motion comes from a loop or helper in the code. **Unroll to edit** turns supported cases into ordinary keyframes.
When a value says **Computed value. Edit it in the Code tab.**, it can only be changed in the code, or ask your agent:

```text theme={null}
Keep the same curved route, but make the move finish with the voiceover instead of two beats later.
```

Good motion reveals, points or connects; text gets time to be read; two unrelated moves don't fight for the same
moment. The code-level rules are in the [GSAP animation guide](/guides/gsap-animation).

## Edit the source

The browser editor, your agent and the CLI all work on the same files. Use **Code** for a small change you understand;
use the agent when it crosses files, changes the structure or starts from an error you don't recognize. (In the
[Studio app](/studio-app/edit-with-the-agent) the agent sits beside the preview, so none of the copying below is needed.)

### Choose the smallest safe surface

| Change | Best starting point |
| - | - |
| Visible text, layout, style, media, timing, or supported motion | Canvas, Inspector, or timeline |
| One known value in one known file | Code |
| Story, several scenes, generated animation, or project structure | Agent |
| A reported lint problem with a clear direct fix | The browser editor or Code |
| An unfamiliar failure or a fix spanning files | Copy to Agent |

The choice is about the change, not a permanent workflow. You can move between
the surfaces without exporting or converting the project.

### Make a focused source edit

1. Open **Code** in the left panel column.
2. Select the exact file in the project tree.
3. Find the value responsible for the visible result.
4. Make one focused change.
5. Wait for the preview to refresh, then play the affected moment.

Edits save automatically and can be undone. If a save fails, the editor says so; fix the connection to the preview
server before going on.

> [!WARNING]
>
> Creating, renaming, moving, or deleting a file can break references elsewhere in the project.
> Search for the old path or ask the agent to update every reference.

Don't edit the same file here and in another tool at once. If the other change lands first, your save is refused with
a message; reload the file, look at what changed, and apply your edit again.

### Ask about the selected element

When a visible element needs source work, select it and choose **Ask agent about
this element**. The browser editor prepares the element and project context, combines it
with your instruction, and copies the prompt to the clipboard. Paste that
prompt into your agent chat.

![HyperFrames browser editor dialog for copying a prompt about the selected element and project context](https://static.heygen.ai/hyperframes-oss/docs/images/studio/ask-agent-v1.jpg)

The browser editor prepares a prompt for the selected element; you paste it into your agent chat.

```text theme={null}
Keep the current narration and scene order. Make this product panel readable
at the final video size, and do not change the following scene.
```

The copied context tells the agent where to look. Your sentence tells it what
must remain true.

### Run Lint

Choose **Lint** at the bottom of the left panel column. The browser editor opens **HyperFrame
Lint Results** with errors, warnings, file locations, and fix hints when they
are available.

Fix a simple, understood issue directly, then run Lint again. Use **Copy to
Agent** when the source location is unfamiliar or the fix may affect other
files. Add what happened before the error and what you expected:

```text theme={null}
This appeared after I shortened the intro clip. I expected the title animation
to keep its current timing. Fix the issue without changing the rest of the
opening.
```

Do not paste only the error message when the intended result matters. A
technically valid repair can still make the wrong creative change.

### Use the project-level gates before delivery

Lint is a quick in-editor pass. The project-level commands remain the
final gate, especially when the project contains nested compositions:

```bash theme={null}
npx hyperframes lint
npx hyperframes check
```

`lint` checks the composition structure. `check` adds browser, runtime, layout,
motion, and WCAG contrast verification.

Passing checks do not approve the story or the final encode. Play the project
after a source fix, then watch the rendered file before sharing it.

### When the preview and source disagree

1. Stop editing until the latest save finishes.
2. Keep the first exact error or save warning.
3. Reload the project only after checking whether another tool changed the file.
4. Run the project checks.
5. Ask the agent with the error, project path, action that caused it, and result
   you expected.

Use [Troubleshooting](/help#in-the-preview-and-browser-editor) for editor, preview, and
render-queue failures. Use [Finish and share](/guides/export-and-share) for the
complete approval, validation, render, and delivery path.

## Related topics

* [Edit timing on the timeline](/studio/timeline)
* [Keyboard shortcuts](/studio/index#keyboard-shortcuts)
* [Recover from a browser editor problem](/help#in-the-preview-and-browser-editor)

# Export and slideshows
Source: https://hyperframes.heygen.com/studio/export

In the browser editor: set up and run renders in the Renders panel, and build a navigable slideshow.

**Export** in the header starts a render straight away, with the settings in the **Renders** panel on the right. So
set those first.

![The Renders panel with format, resolution, frame rate, and quality controls](https://static.heygen.ai/hyperframes-oss/docs/images/studio/export-v1.jpg)

The Renders panel contains delivery settings and the render queue.

## Set up the file

| Setting | Choose |
| - | - |
| **Format** | **MP4** for sharing and uploading; **WebM** for the web and transparent overlays; **MOV** (ProRes) when another editor needs a high-quality master |
| **Resolution** | **Auto** keeps the project's size. Bigger renders are slower and don't sharpen low-resolution footage |
| **Frame rate** | 30 unless the destination or the footage needs 24 or 60 |
| **Quality** | Hidden for MOV, which always uses ProRes quality |
| **Use GPU encoding** | Faster on machines that support it |

**About video formats**, next to the settings, explains the choices.

## The render queue

Each export becomes a row in **Renders**, with its progress. Cancel a running one, download or delete a finished
one, and **Hide finished** to tidy the list without deleting files.

Before sending: open the file itself, watch the start and the end, check captions, cuts and sound at the busiest
moment, and give it a name that says which version it is. If a render fails, keep the error and see
[troubleshooting](/help#in-the-preview-and-browser-editor).

## Build a slideshow

A slideshow is a live, navigable presentation—not one linear video. The **Slideshow** tab appears when the active composition contains a HyperFrames slideshow manifest.

![HyperFrames browser editor showing three main-line slides in the Slideshow panel beside the deck timeline](https://static.heygen.ai/hyperframes-oss/docs/images/studio-slideshow-panel-v1.jpg)

The Slideshow panel builds the main route from real scenes before optional branches are added.

### Build the main path

Start with the route everyone should see:

1. In **Slides**, check the scenes that belong in the main presentation.
2. Use the arrows to put them in order.
3. Select each slide and confirm that it makes one complete point.
4. In **Slide Inspector**, add speaker notes that help the presenter rather than repeat the slide.

The browser editor saves slideshow changes into the project’s manifest. Notes save after a short pause; other edits save immediately and participate in project history.

### Add fragment reveals

Move the playhead to the moment when the presentation should pause, then click **Mark** in Slide Inspector. That time becomes a fragment hold-point for the selected slide.

Use fragments when the presenter needs to reveal part of an idea before advancing. A slide does not need a hold-point for every bullet.

### Add an optional path

Branches keep optional detail outside the main story:

1. Open **Branches**, name a branch, and assign its slides.
2. On the slide where the choice appears, select the visible button or object on the canvas.
3. Open **Hotspot Tool**, choose the target branch, add a useful label, and click **Make hotspot**.
4. Keep a clear route back to the main story.

Deleting a branch removes that branch definition and every hotspot that points to it, so the browser editor asks for confirmation first. The source scenes remain in the project.

### Test it as a presentation

Run the presenter locally:

```bash theme={null}
npx hyperframes present <project-directory>
```

Test next and previous navigation, every fragment, every hotspot, every branch, and the return path. Click **Present** or press **P** to open the synchronized audience view.

> [!NOTE]
>
> A slideshow stays interactive. If the result should simply play from beginning to end as an MP4,
> use a [video workflow](/workflows) instead.

To create the deck with an agent before refining it here, follow [Make an interactive presentation with AI](/guides/slideshow).

## Related topics

* [Render from the command line](/guides/rendering)
* [Finish, render and share](/guides/export-and-share)
* [Make an interactive presentation with AI](/guides/slideshow)
* [Use variables and templates](/studio/assets-and-blocks#use-variables)
* [Work with source and an agent](/studio/canvas#edit-the-source)


# Edit in the browser editor
Source: https://hyperframes.heygen.com/studio/index

The browser editor: open any HyperFrames project with one command and edit what you see, the timing and the motion by hand.

There are two editors. **The [Studio app](/studio-app/index)** is the desktop app with an agent beside the
preview: you say or draw what to change. **The browser editor**, on this page, opens any project folder in your
browser for editing by hand while your own agent works in its terminal. Both edit the same files.

```bash theme={null}
npx hyperframes preview
```

![The HyperFrames browser editor with the Inkwell project open: compositions, preview, Design panel and timeline](https://mintcdn.com/hyperframes/u4Tzq0wRMlm1q5CS/public/images/studio/editor-overview-v2.jpg?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=u4Tzq0wRMlm1q5CS\&q=85\&s=2cf0881c227b1a12bf5a504dc3e547a3)

The browser editor today: files on the left, the preview in the middle, Design on the right, the timeline below. Open in desktop app moves the project to the Studio app.

## Where to start

| You want to change | Start with |
| - | - |
| Something you can see in this frame | Click it in the preview, then **Design** or **Layers** |
| When something appears or how long it stays | The **Timeline** |
| One movement | The animation controls and keyframes |
| The story, several scenes, the structure | Your agent. **Describe a change to the agent** (⌘K) copies a ready request to paste into it |

Panels can be dragged anywhere; **Window** reopens a closed one or resets the layout.

## Edit what you see

Pause where the problem is, click the element (or pick it in **Layers** when things overlap), and change only that.
Drag to move, resize, rotate or crop; use **Design** for text, layout, style, media, motion and color. Then play
through the moment: a frame that looks right can still collide in motion.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Auto-record manual edits as keyframes** is on by default, so a change you make at the playhead becomes animation.
> Turn it off in the timeline toolbar for a fix that should stay the same all the way through.

More: [Edit the frame](/studio/canvas).

## Change the timing

Drag a clip to move it, drag an edge to make it longer or shorter, and use **Split at playhead** to cut one clip in
two. Scrub across the cut after each change. More: [the timeline](/studio/timeline).

## Scrub the preview

Click or drag the seek bar above the preview's playback controls to move through
the video. It stays available with the timeline hidden and in fullscreen. Use
the arrow keys while the seek bar has focus, or Home and End to jump to the
start and end. Seeking pauses playback, just like moving the timeline playhead.

## Check and export

Run **Lint** (bottom left) and fix what it reports, then the full check before you deliver:

```bash theme={null}
npx hyperframes check
```

Choose **Export** in the header, or render from your agent or the command line, and watch the file once before you
share it.

## Keyboard shortcuts

Shortcuts depend on the active area. The table below covers the shortcuts
implemented by the browser editor's player, canvas, and timeline.

### Playback

| Shortcut | Action |
| - | - |
| Space | Play or pause |
| J / K / L | Play backward, stop, or play forward |
| Left / Right arrow | Step one frame, or nudge a selected canvas element horizontally |
| Up / Down arrow | Nudge a selected canvas element vertically |
| Shift + arrow | Step ten frames horizontally, or nudge a selected element farther |
| M | Mute or unmute |
| Shift + L | Toggle loop playback |
| I / O | Set the work-area in or out point |
| Shift + I / Shift + O | Clear the in or out point |
| A / E | Jump to the in or out point |
| F | Toggle fullscreen |

### Editing

| Shortcut | Action |
| - | - |
| V | Selection tool |
| B | Toggle the razor tool |
| S | Split the selected eligible clip at the playhead |
| N | Toggle timeline snapping |
| Command/Ctrl + Z | Undo |
| Command/Ctrl + Shift + Z, or Ctrl + Y | Redo |
| Command/Ctrl + C / V / X | Copy, paste, or cut the selected element |
| Command/Ctrl + G | Group selected elements |
| Command/Ctrl + Shift + G | Ungroup |
| Delete / Backspace | Delete the selected keyframe or element |

The focused area decides what a shared shortcut does. Arrow keys nudge a selected
canvas element, step through frames when nothing nudgeable is selected, or move
between timeline targets when the timeline has focus (see [Timeline
navigation](#timeline-navigation) below). `K` adds or removes a keyframe at the
playhead when a canvas element is selected, starting an animation on a static
element, and otherwise stops playback. `J` always drives playback.

### Timeline navigation

Tab into the timeline before using these commands. The browser editor keeps one logical timeline target in the Tab order and moves that target without requiring every row or clip to stay mounted.

| Shortcut | Action |
| - | - |
| Left / Right arrow | Move to the previous or next target in the focused row |
| Up / Down arrow | Move to the nearest target at the same time in the previous or next logical row |
| Home / End | Move to the start or end of the focused row |
| Command/Ctrl + Home / End | Move to the first or last logical row |
| Page Up / Page Down | Move by one visible page of logical rows |
| Enter / Space | Expand or collapse keyframe property lanes on a focused track row |
| Context Menu or Shift + F10 | Open the focused target's context menu when available |

On an expandable track row, Right arrow expands collapsed keyframe lanes and Left arrow collapses expanded lanes. From a keyframe property row, Left arrow returns to its parent track row. When no disclosure or parent action applies, those arrows continue moving within the row.

If the destination is outside the virtualized viewport, the browser editor scrolls it into view and restores focus after it mounts.

### Keyframes and recording

| Shortcut | Action |
| - | - |
| K | Add or remove a keyframe at the playhead when the current selection supports it |
| R | Start or stop gesture recording |

During gesture recording, drag records position, scroll records depth,
Shift-drag records 3D rotation, Option/Alt-drag records rotation, and
Command/Ctrl-drag or scroll records opacity or scale.

### Canvas and panels

| Shortcut | Action |
| - | - |
| G | Toggle the canvas grid |
| Command/Ctrl + 1 | Open Compositions |
| Command/Ctrl + 2 | Open Assets |
| Option/Alt + drag | Move an entire animation path |
| Shift + drag a resize handle | Resize uniformly |

> [!WARNING]
>
> A shortcut should not fire while you are typing into a text or source field. If the wrong area has focus, click the canvas or timeline before using an editing shortcut.

Use the **Shortcuts and tools** button beside the playback controls for the
built-in shortcut list, work-area controls, and jump-to-frame field.

## Related topics

* [Edit the frame](/studio/canvas)
* [Edit timing on the timeline](/studio/timeline)
* [The Studio app](/studio-app/index)
* [Edit animation and keyframes](/studio/canvas#animate-with-keyframes)


# Edit timing on the timeline
Source: https://hyperframes.heygen.com/studio/timeline

Move, trim, split and align clips in the HyperFrames browser editor, and what each timeline button does.

The timeline sets when each thing appears and how long it stays. Every change saves straight to the project files.

![HyperFrames browser editor timeline with the edge of a selected clip ready to trim](https://static.heygen.ai/hyperframes-oss/docs/images/studio/timeline-v1.jpg)

The selected clip edge changes its duration while the canvas and neighboring tracks remain visible.

## Move, trim, split

* **Move:** drag the middle of a clip. Its length stays the same.
* **Trim:** drag the left edge to change when it starts, the right edge to change when it ends.
* **Split:** put the playhead where you want the cut and choose **Split at playhead**, or press **B** for the Split tool
  and click the clip (Shift-click splits every clip at that time). Press **V** to go back to Select.
* **Copy, Duplicate, Delete:** right-click a clip.

After any change, play across it: entrances, exits and narration don't rewrite themselves.

## The toolbar

| Button | What it does |
| - | - |
| **Linked Selection** | Clicks and edits reach every clip linked to the one you touch, such as a video and its sound |
| **Snapping** | Edges snap to the playhead, other clips and beats |
| **Ripple edit** | On by default: deleting a clip on the main track closes the gap instead of leaving one |
| **Audio meters** | Shows levels while it plays |
| **Add keyframe at playhead** / **Auto-record** | Keyframes for animation; see [animation](/studio/canvas#animate-with-keyframes) |
| **Add beat at playhead** | A timing marker to cut to, handy with music |
| **Select leftward / rightward** (**\[** and **]**, in the tool menu) | Selects every clip that starts before, or after, the playhead, to shift a whole section |

To add media, drop a file on the timeline (**Drop media here**). To work inside a nested scene, expand it or open it
and use the breadcrumb to come back; check whether you're changing its inner timing or its place in the whole video.

Undo (⌘Z) covers moves, trims and splits.

> [accordion] Keyboard and screen reader navigation
>
> Tab into the timeline to reach its current logical focus target. Use Left and Right to move within that row. Use Up and Down to move to the nearest target at the same time in the previous or next row.
>
> Home and End move to the start or end of the focused row. Hold Command or Ctrl to move to the first or last logical row. Page Up and Page Down move by one visible page of rows.
>
> On an expandable track row, Right expands collapsed keyframe property lanes and Left collapses expanded lanes. From a keyframe property row, Left returns to its parent track row. Enter or Space toggles the same lanes. Use the Context Menu key or Shift + F10 to open the focused target's menu when it has one.
>
> The timeline keeps only one logical timeline target in the Tab order. Native header controls, such as visibility and keyframe actions, remain separate Tab stops. When the logical target is outside the virtualized viewport, the browser editor keeps it mounted, scrolls it into view, and then restores focus.
>
> Screen readers receive the timeline as a treegrid. Track rows announce their level and expanded state. Clips and keyframes announce their names, times, and selection state. Easing controls announce their names and times.
>
> The full list is in [keyboard shortcuts](/studio/index#timeline-navigation).

* [Edit animation and keyframes](/studio/canvas#animate-with-keyframes)
* [Keyboard shortcuts](/studio/index#keyboard-shortcuts)
